BOFOUGH OF ST. TIELENS.—HER MAJESTY'S JUBILEE. At a meeting of the Town Council of this Borough, held on the Bth day of April, 1887, the following recommendations of the Special Committee appointed to report to the Council on this subject, were adopted. viz : That Sec Majesty's Jubilee be celebrated in this Borough in the following manner :- 1. That a prooesaion through the town to the Peak be or- panLsod, in which the local 'Volunteers, the lire Brigade, tad the School Children be invited to join. 2. That on the arrival of the procession at the Park the Mayor be asked to publfcly name ft "Th. Yictorta Park." .

3, That a grant be made to each Elementary Day School represented after the rate of ed. for each scholar In the pro- oession who is on the school register, for the purpose of Providing refreshments for the children. 4. That a medal be presented to each scholar in the pro- cession. 5. That a dinner to 500 aged poor be given. 6. That there be a display of fireworks. 7. That refreshments be provided for the Volunteers, Pollee, and Fire Brigade in the prooess'on. The Aldermen and Councillors for each Ward will Act as a Local Committee for the collection of subscriptions to cover the expenditure, and donations may be paid either to them or to either of the local banks. - - - - SHE DOESN'T KNOW CHICKEN FROM TURKEY."* Helene is the handsomest girl of her race— She's an elegant form and an exquisite face, And she dresses with perfectly consummate grace, But she doesn't know chicken from turkey. She knows many languages, living and dead; In science and fiction is very well read, But she eannottoolemeatrand she cannot make bread, And she doesn't know chicken from turkey. She can play a fantasia or nocturne with skill, Can sing up to B—has a wonderful trill; Can write a good story or sonnet, but still She doesn't know chicken from turkey. • She's been up the Tiber, the Rhine, and the Nile; She's a painter in every popular style— Can decorate china, a plaque, or a tile— But she doesn't know chicken from turkey. She's always self-satisfied, graceful, and cool; A critic both just and correct, as a rule, And knows every stitch of the Kensington School, But she doesn't know chicken from turkey. She can work a design by a Lensing or Burt; But she cannot cut out for her children a skirt, Or make for her husband a well-fitting shirt— She doesn't know chicken from turkey. I'm willing a brirl shgula read Latin and Greek; Should German and French and Italian speak; And be "up" in the latest testhetical freak, If she only knows chicken from turkey. f I'd like her in Music and song to take part; Read poetry, science, and cultivate art, If husband and children were first in her heart, And if she knew chicken from turkey— Knew barley from rice, knew a tart from a pie; A boil from:a:stew, a broil from a fry; And if she went into the market to buy, Knew very well chicken from turkey. For to make a home happy all knowledge must blend Art, science, and service tbeir benefitsdend ; Then, ladies so clever and wise,. condescend To know about chicken and turkey. ',An old saying for a poor housewife.

When it rains hardest —When it hails. A question of time.—The erection of public clocks. Idleness is the key of beggary and the root of all evil. A traveller recently returned from Flowery Land says that the Chinese do not eat mutton chops with chop- sticks. NEEDING NO BUSH.—Host "Well, my boy, this is some- thing like wine, isn't It?" Guest reflectively: "Yes. What is it ?" A gentleman of this city has a small boy. When a friend called recently the father said to him politely, "I wish I had another cigar to offer you," looking with regret at the one he was smoking. Now was the small boy's opportunity. "I know- where they are, pa," he said, dragging open a drawer and bringing out a box of a choice brand. A merchant cannot be successful who has no " business enterprise." Although we may differ with this one or that one as to what'is business enterprise, or may differ with the German grocer whose opinion of enterprise is stated below, we cannot doubt that Hans had something in his head besides beer. "What is the price of sausages ?" asked a customer. "Dwenty cents a pound" was the ansvier. "You asked twenty-five this morning." "'fah, dot vos ven I had some. Now I ain't got none I sells him for dwenty cents. Dot makes me a reputation for selling cheab, und I don'd lose noddings." Those (says Lord William Lennox) who liked a witty remark or a pungent epigram would join the table at -which James Smith sat, and any commonplace remark of the day was immediately committed by him into verse. I remember once asking him if he was going to the ball at the Mansion House, got up in aid of the unfortunate Polish refugees. "No," he said. Then. call- ing for a sheet of paper and a pencil, he wrote the fol- lowing lines:— Aloft, in rotatory motions hurled, The Poles are called on to support the world. In 'these our dads a different law controls; The world is called on to support the Poles. Writing lines is the pennance Harrow boys do for all their sins, in and out of school. If a boy is late for school, he Writes lines; if he misses "bill," he writes lines. If the lines are not finished at a stated tim-. their number is doubled. There was one clever boy who escaped writing half the ordered quantity; and the masters tell the story of how he did it to this day. He was an untidy boy, and was often taken to task for his carelessness and disorder. One day his master, who had very dignified and impres- sive manners, and who always said "we" instead of "you" when talkinp.',i•to the boys, found occasion to re- prove him. "We do not look very clean," he said, with much severity. "We have not washed our hands this morning. Have we ?" "I don't know about yours," was the impudent boy's answer, "but I've washed mine." Ah!" said the master, "we are very impertinent to- day. W will have to write a hundred lines before the next bill." When "bill" time came, the master sent for the boy. "Have we written- ourlines ?" he asked. 'l've written my fifty," the boy answered very promptly, handing in his paper, "but I don't know whether you b we done your half I" LIQUID FUEL EXPERIMENTS.—Last autumn (says En- gineering) the Russian Government adopted a new type of liquid furnace, invented by Lieut. Pashinin, for the torpedo boat Lerke. Experimental trips befgre the close of the season demonstrated the success of the new invention; but no details were published as to the re- sults obtained. Since then the same furnace has been fitted to two steamers built by the firm of Butz and Co., St. Petersburg, for service on the river Oxus. A trial with these took place a few days ago, in the presence of a large number of influential personages, and, according to the Naves Vrestya, was again a complete success. The trial demonstrated that 11b. of petroleum refuse evapo- rated 15.61 b. of water, or 2* times more than coal. Dur- ing the consumption of the liquid fuel, a sheet of white paper was held at a height of 14in. above the funnel, and at the end was neither discoloured nor marked with traces of, aopt. Compared with other systems in use in Russia, the .‘'Kovoe Vrentya says that whereas the propor- tion between the „espenditure of cafil and oil refuSe is 2 to 3, the proportion in the new invention is/ to Pro- , bably further practice will iatid to better resulet than even- Mese; OS at present, 'oreigg to the low price of liquid -fatel,-Riissian engineers have no inducements to be economic:O.. At Baku the price per ton is often as low as 4d., and the question of economy is never thaight sof at all. On the Volga, however, the case is different, and the farther.Aons Bakuathe more careful the en- gineers are found to be. It is expected that Pashinin's furnace will' be applied tlis year to a largexaimber of torpedo' boats in the Black Seat where the supply of liquid fuel is now plentiful. ' Mr. Clark son, a North-Country gentleman some eighty- five years old, who surveyed the railway between Leeds and Derby under George Stevenson, recently related an incident connected with that period. Mr. Clarkson,said he remembered Stevenson calling all the engineers to- gether at the end a their survey at the Tontine Hotel, Sheffield. At the conclusion of the business Mr. Steven- son, in a merry mood, mounted the coach for London. "Now," said George, addressing the mail-coach driver and guard, "what's to be done with you saucy fellows when these grand railways are completed?" "Well, Mr. Stevenson," said the ready-witted driver, "I don't know; you'll just have to make civil engineers of us." MOST FELLOWS Kisow.—When Mr. Jenkins went to his bedroom at half-past one, it was with the intention of going to sleep, and with another determination, that.he would not be interviewed by Mrs. Jenkins. Sc, as soon as he had entered the door and deposited his lamp upon the dressing table, he commenced his speech I locked the front door. I put the chain on. I pulled the key out a little bit. The dog is inside. I put the kitten out. I emptied, the drip-pan of the refrigerator. The cook took the s .Dver faked with her. put akane tindeilhe knob of the back liardoor. I put the fastenings over the bath-room windows. The parlour fire has coat on. I put the cake box back in Pe closet. I did not oktnk all the milk. tt. i not goingwto rain. NTabOdy gave me any message for you. I mailed your letters as soon as I got down town. -.Youn*other did not call at the office. Nobody died that:„we fire intexested in. - Did not hear of a marriage or engagement. I was very busy at the office making out bills. I lave liting nky clethes.over chair backs. Mondock Bay, on th' Peninsula o' Arpley, is a haven it wud puzzle a many ancient mariners furt find i' ther charts, an' fur those that know it it requires a bit o' gumption furt get theer fro' East- him ith' nick o' time. Aw thowt bi ther talk th' chaps didn't altogether like th' look o things. They sed it wodn't do furt start too soon afore ther was plenty o' waater'furt rhow in; an' upoth' other hand t' wudn't do t' let too much waater goo an ath banks covert; ther'd bi sich a say on an wi mought be too late get under Woughton Bridge. It reminded mi oth' wench when hoo wur gooin' t' meet her lover. "Aw conna fur shawm bi too soin, an' aw wudn't forth world bi too late." Na th' sun ed gett'n hee ith' sky an' wus sheddin his mornin' glory on these Eastham woods, NVOSO sheltrin pre- sence wi was loath to leuf. Here th' gold'n beams oth' sun med beautiful the verdure o' the trees an' showed wi glorious distinctness each interlacing branch. As if furt intensify th' antithesis oth' calm below, th' topmost boos wur writhin' an' ben- din' like corn before th' wind. An' th' little brids wur singin' merrily ith' woo 4. Wi cud yeer um na an' then ith' pauses oth' roar fro' th' tree tops. Below, an' inshore, things wore a quiet an' peacefu' look; but ateside wi cud see th' banks fringed wi white breakers, an' flats gooin' up wi'very smaw sails on um, but scutterin' away i' fine style. So it wur abaate time wi wur shapin' fur worn. Wid cum da'an wi a wole sail, but it wudn't do furt try t' goo up wi one; so th' chaps seet to an' took two reefs in. Then they geet a poo upoth main halyerds, an' seet th' luff taut, but kept th' peak settled. Then they clapt on to th' cable an' hove short, and waited furth' word "up anker." Wen they'd pood it clear oth' graand, they seet th' fosle an' cast her yed to th' South, an' run alung shore tuth eend o' Eaatham bank. Aye! an' its vary nice abaate theer fine weather. Under th' Boostance wood, an' abaate th' owd cow shed an' Poo Haw wood! Its one oth' trials life furt leeuv this lovely spot, wi its sweet sunimer seents an' sects, an' its clear saut water, furt go into th' nasty sink slutch they cawn water at Warriton. Wi cawnt sing "Home, sweet home," wi ony sense (Ali fitness o' things if wi thinken oth' river which " &red to emulate a classic tide," but now •" creeps filth laden through. empoisoned towns." 'Things are sadly changed sin th' "classic tide" bisness wus theer. Well, wen wid getten to th' cow-shed wi run into th' "fret "fort wait tin th' waater wur a bit heier furt cross th' bank. So infatuated was he with it that Lady Cozen—though she liked it, too—began to be alarmed at his extra- vagance, and her alarm was not without reason, for he ran himself seriously in debt in constructing a palace luxurious enough for a man with three times his means. Lord Cozen had spent some £70,000 in the purchase and decoration of this place when its previous owner, Jack Joiner, suddenly died. He had survived the sale of his parental abode only two years, and no one who knew his habits were surprised at that. Probably, if there were any surprise going, it was that he had lived so long. His father had accumulated an immense fortune in trade, which the son had dissipated in pleasure. Making it had killed the fatherat fifty; spending it had killed the son at thirty-five. It WM some months after his death that a stranger called upon Lord Cozen at his country seat. He declined to give the servant his names, When his lordship went into the library to see him,she thought the stranger resembled someone he had seen before, but who it was his lordship could not tell., , "Well, my lord," said the stranger, speaking with a slight American twang, "you have made this a fine place to what it was."

Lord Cozen looked surprised. This, he thought, was an extraordinary beginning. "Yes" said his lordship, coldly; "I have spent a good deal of money on it," "So I should guess," said the stranger. "It was very kind of you. Might I ask the amount?" "May I ask," replied Lord Cozen, angrily, "what busi- ness it is of yours ?" "Oh, certainly. Because the place is mine." " Yours ! Are you out of your wits, sir? If you have , nothing but this to tell me, leave this minute, or I'll have you turned out." "Not so fast, my lord, not so fast. Let me tell you it Is I that will turn you out. Do you know who lam ?" "No, nor do I care." "Oh, yes, you do, though I dare say you don't know it. Well, I'm J,oe Joiner, brother of the late Jack." It now occurred to Lctrd Cozen that that was the per- son of whom the stranger had reminded him. "Well," said his lordship, after a pause, "what is that to me? Your brother sold me the place." "All. yes; but it wasn't his to selL He had only a life interest in it, which is now," and the stranger gave a sigh, "terminated." " What ? Are you come here to blackmail me—to extort money from me by questioning my title? If you

"But I'm not. I'm only stating the truth. See here. This is a copy of my fathers's will. D'ye see that?—' To my eldest son, John, for life—hum—issue--hum—and in default of issue to Joseph, my second son.' What do you say to that?" "It is a forgery !—a fraud! Where did this supposed will come from "From Somerset House, where you could have seen it if you had wished." "My God! But your btother told me that he was an only child, and that his father died intestate !" "Ah ! Jack was always a liar !" 'But I have doubled—quadrupled—the value of this place." "That is exactly why I said your lordship was so kind." "But you don't mean to say that you're going to con- fiscate the impr3vemfintB which have cost me so much ?" "lam going to eqpfiscate nothing. What the law says belongs to me is mine. I claim nothing but what the law gives me." " Infamous ! This may be law, but it's not justice." "1 cannot,argue with you. I dare say you and I have very different notions of what is justice, but we both know whit's the law. It is well+ to abide by what is certain. My lord, I wish you a very good morning. You'll get the writ to-morrow."

div.head: CRADLEY HEATH CHAINMAKERS.
div.p: THE CRADLEY HEATH CHAIN- MAKERS.

On Saturday evening a meeting was held in the Co-operative Hall, Warrington, in furtherance of the efforts that are being made in the town in aid of the distressed chainmakers of Cradley. There was a pretty good attendance of working-men, those present being fairly representative of the different industries and works of the town. The chair was filled by Mr. H. Whitham, and amongst others present was Mr. Homer chairman of the Chainmakers' Association, who gave a graphic des- cription of the sufferings of the "white slaves of Cradley." The CHAIRMAN, in the course of a short introduc- tory address, urged that the great need of the time was the devising of some machinery which would make it impossible for such a state of things as that at Cradley to exist. Even if the workmen were successful in their present struggle, there would at once begin to be a tendency back to the old state of things. What they had to complain against most was not the legitimate manufacturers, who con- ducted their establishments in a fairly reasonable way, but a class of men who are termed " foggers," who came in and underbid the other employers. The fo,ggers came in and got hold of the poorest class of workmen and then undersold other manufact- turers. It was this state of thingsthat wanted alter- ing, and it could only be altered by a strong com- bination. (Applause.) He was in favour not so much of labour fighting capital as seeking to get the control of capital into its own hands. (Hear, hear.) Those who laboured should have some of the profit, but at the same time under present condi- tions employers were not to blame .because they _ _ . .

/ere to Sortie extent the victims of circumstance, Hear, hear, and applause.) Mr. T. FLOOD next moved a resolution calling upon the Government to make some inquiry into the methods of working carried en at 'Cradley, Heath and district, and insisting that the employ- ment of females in the chain trade tends to degrade labour and lower the Workmen's wages. (Applause.) Mr. Flood referred to a description he had recently ' heard of the sufferings of the chainmakers, and said that if they had heard those harrowing details they would scarcely believe that these poor chainmakers were living within a short distance of what he might perhaps call the largest centre of industry in the country, and within the shadow' of teeming wealth and affluence. (Hear, hear.) He urged upon working-men the necessity of bringing their nfluence to bear on members of Parliament in re- gard to matters of the kind they were there to dis- cuss, and remarked that if the industry of the country was to be maintained a responsibility rested on the Government or legislative body to see that it slid not decay for want of attention on the part of the legislature. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Mr. DUN, in seconding the proposition, said he agreed with the chairman as to the necessity of strong combinatien amongst workingmen, though he was the last man to wish to encroach upon the just rights of any employer he'might. have to work for. (Applause.) Mr. Homan, the chairman of the Chainmakers' Association, next addressed the meeting. He was sorry, he said, that he should have to appear before them, or any audience of 'workingmen, to relate what he had about the condition of any class of workmen. It was a disgrace and shame to human- ity that such a state of things should ever be brought about, and be allowed to remain in exist- ence so long as it had done. (Hear, hear.) He was almost afraid to describe the condition of things at Cradley Heath and district, He himself had worked at chainmaking for some years, until it got into what they then considered a bad state, but nothing like what it is now. At that time they got 5s 3d per cwt. for making the kind of chain which he showed to the audience, but since then the price had been reduced time after time till it came down to lOid per cwt. (" Shame.") The diffioulty was to get people to believe the truth as to the state of things at Cradley Heath. Ile then gave some details as to the earnings of chainmakers, and said that they had to work hard to make Ss 9d a week, and out of that 2s ed had to be paid for assistance. He asked I them if that was sufficient for a hard-working man to live upon. (" No.") It was very hard work, for nearly every muscle had to be brought into play, and Urn there were the effects of a hot fire to stand, which made the workman throw off a lot of perspiration. He therefore required more than an ordinary amount of food, if he was to labour from Monday morning till Saturday night. The people had been reduced so low that he was ashamed to tell them what he had seen. There were scores of the women who- had sold their very wedding rings, and the furnitnre had been sold bit by bit till there were hundreds of people who had no beds to to lie upon, and the beds that others had got were not worthy the name of beds. If one went into the houses the wretchedness and misery were most appalling to look at. If they saw the men at their work They would wonder how they got through were wiry, and they had it, but though little they also been trained to the work. Referring to the truck system, Mr. Homer said it was quite rampant till he went amongst the chainmakers. The great difficulty they had had in connection with trucking was to bring home a conviction. If a man gave any information by which a master was convicted of trucking that man was marked ; there was no more work for that man, he might as well bury himself alive or be transported to some other part of the world. (Hear, hear.) But in spite of these difficulties he was thankful to say that within the last nine months they had accomplished a great deal, and he considered that the putting down of the truck system would be a glorious victory. (Hear, hear.) He did not look upon the present stoppage of work as a strike in the ordinary sense

div.head: AN EVICTOR EVICTED.
div.p: AN EVICTOR EVICTED.

-Lord Cozen drew every shilling of his income from Ireland, and spent every shilling of it in England. For acting in this way he had various reasons, of which his being fond of England and his Irish tenantry not being fond of him were probably the principal. He was a care- less, pleasure-seeking gentleman, who liked living com- lortably, and disliked running the risk ef being shot at. He took no pride in his position as a great territorial lord; in fact, he hated to hear any reference to the twenty thousand acres he possessed. If it had not been for the income with which they supplied him, he would have wished them miles Under the sea. 'The administration of his immense estates he left ab- solutely in the hands of his agent, Mr. Peter Stoney, with this: solitary direction: that he should get as much rent out of them as he could. That direction Mr. Stoney never for a moment forgot. Though it. was very con- cise, it revealed to the astute agent h great deal. It showed him in what light his lordship regarded his pro- perty, what consideration he had for his tenants, and how his agents could best win his approbation. So, under Mr. Stoney's management, the Cozen estates became the most remarkable in Ireland for moonlighting, evictions, and high rents, and the agent was cited by their owner as being a model man of business. 4. Neighbouring landlords, however, who did not share his lordship's income' did not approve so much of Mr. Stoney's behaviour. In fact, the majority of them were annoyed and disgusted at it. Some objected to it because it created continual trouble in the neighbourhood and kept the poor-rates up; others because the discontent it caused often spread to neighbouring estates, and led the tenants to demand reductions from rents they might otherwise have paid ; while some few others, who had a dim and glimmering notion about property having its duties as well as its rights, were opposed to it less on in- terest than on principle. It was with these last that Lord Cozen was most angry. Whets they remonstrated with him on his harsh behaviour and his absenteeism, he would tell them to mind their own business; he sup- posed that, although he did own some land, he could live where he pleased and do what he liked with his own. A pauper might do that, and so, he presumed, might a peer. His lordship did live where ,he pleased—in London— and he did do what he liked with his own. He was a bachelor, with a taste for pleasure which his income (thanks to Mr. Stoney) enabled him to gratify. His companions voted him a brick, and his tradesmen were delighted to see his face, for he was careless and profuse in his expenditure. It is true that his cash was not used very properly. The money earned by the sweat of many a poor man's brow, and taken from the mouths of many a starving wife and child, was thrown away on cham- pagne suppers, on diamonds for low-class actresses, and on the turf. But in the same way as his lordship cared little how he came by his money, he cared little how it went from him. Not long since his lordship's already ample income was considerably increased. His uncle by marriage, Sir Charles Kinderly, died, and under his will Lord Cozen, became entitled to another estate in Ireland of several thousand acres. The new estate contrasted strangely with the old. The latter, devoted principally to use of a few graziers, lay almost entirely uncultivated, while the people who should have been tilling it were wretched cottiers spending their lives in rags and idle- ness. The new land, on the other hand, was like a market garden. Divided into small farms of twenty or thirty acres each, it supported a numerous population in industry, comfort, and prosperity. Sir Charles had been a model landlord and a kindly gentleman. Early in life he had married a sister of Lord Cozen's mother, but his bride died only a few months a fter the marriage, and he, heartbroken and hopeless, had retired from the world to spend the remainder of his long life on his estate and among his people. His chief object henceforth was the happiness of his tenantry. To increase their comfort, and to teach them industry and thrift, was the goal to which he directed all his efforts. At first he endeavoured to accomplish this by spend- ing considerable sums of money on improving their farmhouses and in draining their lands; but he received little encouragement or co-operation from his people in the task. Seeing the failure of this means, he tried another. He gave each of his tenants a lease for a hundred years of his farm at a moderate rent. The result was niervelidus. Without his spending a penny or making an exertion, he saw his estate rapidly become the best drained, best cultivated, and most fer- tile for forty miles round. New and comfortable houses quickly took the place of mud cabins, industry and thrift of idleness and improvidence, prosperity and con- tent of misery and agitation. The kindly gentleman was nearly as much surprised at the result of his ex- periment as he was delighted. He never tired of going about his land, watching every improvement, and encouraging and advising his tenants, among whom he was regarded with a reverence and affection unfortu- nately vouchsafed to few landlords in Ireland, and not deserved by many. Though their leases, they were aware, made it to them a matter of no importance, from a pecuniary point of view, who their landlord was, yet when his death removed his aged presence from among them, they deplbred his loss as much as if their existence had depended upon him. When Lord Cozen succeeded to the property, the only feeling with which the leases inspired him was one of disgust. He cared nothing that they had been the means of transforming an estate of bog-lands and grazing- ground into the most fertile district in the province, and a population of starving and discontented cottiers into a prosperous and quiet peasantry. All that he looked to was the fact that they diminished the rent, and that they prevented him levying a confiscatory tax upon the improvements which the tenants themselves had tnado, When Mr. Peter Stoney told him that, but foe these leases, his income might be increased by four or five thousand a year, it is to be feared that his lordship used language concerning Sir Charles Kinderly which was not parliamentary, nor becoming the lips of an heredi- tary legislator. Lord Cozen was still mourning over what he called his uncle's folly, when he received a letter from his agent which startled and delighted him. It appeared from it that Mr. Peter Stoney, while discharging for his lordship the duties of executor to Sir Charles, had found among the deceased's papers a marriage-settlement. That settle- ment had been drawn up years ago, previous to Sir Charles's union with the younger Miss Lynch. Lord Cozen's father was then only,a younger sop, with a very limited allowance, but he had the adVantege of being the husband of the quondam elder Miss Lynch. The younger Miss Lynch did not forget this when the settlements in view of her marriage with Sir Charles Kinderly were being drawn up. Cold-blooded and grasping, like all the Lynches, she had insisted that not merely she and her children should be provided for, but that her sister and hers should be looked after too. She required that after the usual limitations to Sir Charles and herself and the issue of their marriage, the estate should be settled upon , her sister Clara—Lord Cozen a mother—and her issue. Sir Charles had no near relatives, and he was deeply enamoured of his financee, so without demur he consented to the settlement being made as she desired. Sir Charles evidently attached little importance to the document It had been drawn up privately, and was apparently communicated not even to Lord Cozen's mother, since Lore Cozen himself had never heard of it. As its primary object had been to provide for the issue of his marriage, probably 4r Xharles, on his wife's death, considered that it bad bectmee invalid.. At any rate, he acted as if he believed this, and though under it he had power to trrake no lease for over thirty-five years, he had, as haa been said, gra.hted to every tenant a lease for a hundred yeers. "He must have thought these leases good, or he Would never have Made them. - Mr. Deter .Stoney, however, ,knew differently. The limitation to the sister and her issue was:just as binding 'as ever 'lifter Lady Kinderly's death.. Lord Cozen was entitled to the estate independently of the will under the settlement, and Tirei7 lease for over thirty-five years -granted by Mir Charles was invalid as against him. When this fact became known among the tenants, it can easily be imagined the consternation it created. All their leases were bad! TheN would not believe it. It was, they felt sure, a report, a lying report, set abroad by that scoundrel Peter Stoney to frighten them. He thought to scare them into permitting some modification of their positioe, some increase in their rents. But he would discover his 'Mistake.. He would find that they were men net to be-frightened by false fire. Their courage cooled, hOwever, when one fine morning every man on the estate found himself served with a writ of ejectment. • HOUSE OF LORDS —MONDAY I • , The Lord Chancellor took his seat at 420 p.m. Sionan ABATEMENT.—On the motion for the second reading of the Smoke Nuisance Abatement (Metropolis) Bill, which measure had 'seen introduced in their lord- ships' House by Lord Stratheden and Campbell, the Duke of WESTMINSTER and Lord Mourn TEMPLE gave a general support to the bill. Lord SALISBURY said the Govern- ment would not oppose the second reading, but sug- gested that a sufficient time should be given for a con- sideration of its details before the committer stage was taken; and Lord GiteNvrtar was understoo,i to suggest that the bill should be referred to a Select Committee.— The bill was read a second time. FORGSD SIGNATURES TO VOTING PAPERS.—Lord MONKS- WELL drew attention to the wholesale forgery of signa- tures to voting papers which was alleged to have taken place at Chatham at the recent election to the Local Board of Health, and asked whether the Local Govern- ment Board would inquire into the conduct of that elec- tion?—Lord BALFOUR of Buntnicur said the Local Government Board had no jurisdiction to hold an in- quiry into such a subject, but any person who was aggrieved bad a remedy under the Public Health Act. IRISH COUNTY COURT BUtING.—The Duke Of ARGYLL afterwards referred to certain recent rulings of Judge Curran, and was informed by Lord FITZGERALD that the judge had done nothing morc C.inei he was empowered to do.
7The House. adjourned at 5 n 5 p.m. HOUSE OF COMMON.—MOI4DAY.

TH. RRECT lON IN AniNANISTAN.-,.. answer to Sir H. Tyler, said: The insurrection of (Ail- 'iSis in Afghanistan is still proceeding, and engagements haVe taken place in which each side claims the victory, but there is no reason to think that the Ameer is not holding his own. The defences of Herat have recently been Strengthened by the Ameer. No plan for extending the Quettah Railway to Candshar has yet been adopted. THE " TlIsfES ' AND THE PA HNELLITES.—A Pkasostat _ _
- STATEMENT.—Mr. I. O'CON,WOR asked leave to .make a.

personal statement, It appeared to him, from the posi.' tion they had taken up, that the Goyernment were per- fectly willing to make party capital out of allegations 'and insinuations such as had appeared in The Times. In these circumstances he had thought it proper to himself and to his colleagues to refuse any longer to serve on the Royal Commission on the Civil Service, and he had Intimated to the chairman his desire that he should take steps to cause his name to be removed from the mem• bership of the commission. THE CRIMES BILL.

The House then went into Committee on the Criminal Law Amendment (Ireland) Bill. Some amendments haring been ruled out of order, an amendment was agreed to by the Government provid• leg that the preliminary inquiry, should be held at the petty sessional court of the district in which the offence

occurred. NU. 'f. M. HEALY moved an amendment tn provide that the witness to be examined in the pre!" ry inquiry should be "summoned in the prescriLA, —inner," the object being that the summons should state the place of Inquiry, the name of the magistrate, and the crime with regard to which evidence was desired. The ATTORNEY-GENERAL for IRELAND declined_ to

accept the amendment. If it were adopted it would be impossible to bring witnesses except by summons. With permission, Mr. Healy altered the form of his amendment, providing that the witness should attend "on summons," simply, instead of that "he should be summoned in the prescribed form." The Committee divided, when there voted—

For the amendment 139 Against An amendment by Mr. FOWLER required that the wit- ness examined should be a person whom the resident magistrate "has reason to believe to be capable of giving material evidence concerning the offence," was agreed to, as was also one standing to the name of Mr. Pdaruni to the effect that the witness lihotild not he "a person con- fessing himself or herself to be the offender, or the hus- -I?and or wife of such person." Mr. T. HRA.LY proposed that the resident magistrate should be compelled to take the deposition of the witness. The Alrouszy-GENERAL at first said he thought the resident magistrate should. be allowed to exercite his . . .

discretion; but after some discussion he intimated that the Government did not attach much importance to the matter, and rather than encourage prolonged debate .would accept the anienditient. (Parnelfite cheers.) Several amendments having been withdrawri or nega- tived; an amendment by Mr. Hasty, that a shorthand writer should be in attendance at the inquiries, and should take down the questions of the magistrate and the answers of each witness, was accepted by the Government. ' Mr.' Hharr Ulm moved an, amendment providing that ft persoh, on being returned for trial, should be supplied with copies of all depositions taken at an inquiry under this section. Sir p..licssin.r. suggested that the accused should be

supplied with the depositions of any witness to be called ,against him, and moved the addition of words to that !affect to the amendment—The amendment, having been modified, was agreed to. ••• Mr.MARMINGT6N moved the insertion cot aw provision 'that the' examination .should be conducted in such a ,ffistffner only ae it would be conducted if such person were giving evidence in support of a charge against some person for committing the offence in respect of which the inquiry was held.—The Arroron3Y-GmERAL • for IRELAND said the Government were unable to accept the proposal, as it would unduly restrict the inquiry, which the clause already provided must relate to a specific offence.—The Committee divided : For the amendment 193 , • Against

A long wrangle then TOO-i-i;l:a-ce--a-sTo-i:e.P.orting pro- gress. Mr. W. H. Smith pressed the Committee to finish the sub-section. Discussion on an amendment by Mr. Healy was continued till 2 0 a.m., when another attempt was made by the 'lrish members, supported by the Radical members, to induce the Government to report

_ progress. Mr. Healy rising at 245 to continue the discussion, Mr. W. H. Swim, amid cries of "Shame" from the Irish members, moved" :that the question be now put."—Mr. Healy rose to speak, but was instantly called to order. The Committee divided— For putting the question 249 4g41p1t..0...., 4.... 1.70-49 Great amusement was created by the Chairman naming Mr. Healy and Mr. J. Morley as the tellers against I.the motion. Mr. Morley evidently refused to act, as, after a communication. from Mr. Arnold Morley, Mr. Healy and Mr. Cox were named as tellers. , The amendment under di:ten-zinc was then put, and, upon a division, was rejected by 2.) to 150. Mr. LABOCCHERE moved to report progress.—The Committee divided—For, 170; against, 248. Mr. R. WALLACE moved that the Chairman do now . . . _

leave the chair.—Mr. Conybenre was speaking in film- port of the motion. when Mi. W. H. Smrrn rnmied ?that the question be nowput."—The Committee divided— For the closure Against The Committee then divided on the motion that the Chairman do leave the chair. , • For the 'motion ' lB2 Against _245-83

Mr. W. Ff. SMITH moved the Words skiown to I' enact- ment," which is the second word of the second section, be now nut. The CHAIRMAN declined to put the closure, bac' amid of the six amendments it. Would exclude from ditonsirion. There were two which he thought ought to be discussed for some time. Sir C. RIISSRLL moved an amendment confihing exam- ination of witnesses to the offence being inquired into, and not to any other subject Whatever, The ATTORNEY-GxvrnAL opposed the amendment.— The Committee then divided—

For the amendment 165 Against . The next amendment was by Mr. T. Healy, but was not pressed. The closure resolution was agreed to, and the first two words of the second section were put and agreed to. . Progress was then reported amid cheers. THE OATHS BTLL. Mr. BnAntatron Moved the second reading of the Oaths Bill.

Mr. DE LISLE moved that the House do now adjourn. —Mr. Bnaotarou said he would only, take a division for the purpose of showing who were against the BilL— SirE. CLARKE deprecated a division being taken on that condition, and hoped the sec3nd reading would be agreed to. _

Mr. STANLEY Lsionvoic censored the Government for the weakness they were displaying. The House divided. For the adjournrhent 1' 104 Against 195-91 The announcemeritettidertun2hera was received with &eel's:—

• Sir J. FERGUSSON hoped that a division wOuld be taken against the second reading.—Colenel EIUGHES thought ft would be a subject of deep regret if an appeal to a Supreme Being were dispensed with in our law courts. --Mr. 13. BYRON REED moved the adjournment of the debate.—Mr. BRADLAI,OII briefly opposed the motion for adjournment.—After a short discussion the House divided, and the motion for adjournment was defeated by 111 to 87. Mr. MARK STEWART moved the adjournment of the Roma—Mr. BRADLATIGH was satisfied with the two majorities in favour of the principle of the bill.—The motion for the adjournment of the House was withdrawn, and the debate was adjourned.
The Licensed Pretnises (Entire Closing,) (Scotland) Bill was read a second time. -
- The House adjourned at 5 50 a.m.
HOUSE OF LORDS.-Ty.

The Lord-Fh.a-,rl-e-lk;r-took his seat at 4 15 P.m. BILLS ADVANCED.—The Bankruptcy Offices (Sites) Bin was read a second time.—The Local Government Pro- visional Orders Bill was read a third time,..and passed. VIIVOTAL OF AN EDUCATIONAL ENDOW/CERT.—Me Arch- bishop of YORK moved an address to the'Crown, praying her Majesty to withhold her consent from the scheme of Charity Commissioners for the management of the Free

Grammar School and Hospital at Bemsworth, in York- shire. Hemsworth, he said, was a cluster of colliery villages, and the opinion of the locality was, decidedly opposed to the removal to Barnsley of this educational endowment, which was of the value of £450 a year.— Lord MiturowN seconded the motion.—Earl Srancan stated that the scheme was submitted to the Educa-
tional Committee of the Privy Council- last year, and it was shown on conclusive evidence that

the school, which was founded in 1548 by a charter of Henry VIII. had been in recent years a failure, and an inquiry on the spot satisfied the Com- missioners that it was litllo or no use maintaining it at Hemsworth.—Lord CrRIMTHORPE supported that ad- dress, and described Hemsworth as a healthy oasis in a desert of blackness.—Lord ST. OSWALD, thS one of the trustees of the school, objected to the removal, and Lord COLCHESTER spoke in favour.—Lord PENMAN added a few words, amidst loud cries for a division, which drew from him the defiant question, "Which noble lord dared to say 'divide' ?"—Their lordships divided, and the numbers were—for the address 38, against 61, majority 23. Casstericm—Lord Forum moved for a return of the number of cremations that have taken place in England within the last five years, and asked by what authority and under what regulations they were permitted.—The Marquis of SALISBURY said cremation was in individual discretion, and no record was accessible to the Govern- ment of the number of times the practice had been put in use. He should doubt whether there was the danger of the concealment of mineral poisoning that the noble lord seemed to apprehend, and the practice was hardly sufficiently common at present to call for Parliamentary interference.—The Earl of MlLT:rows observed that there was nothing illegal in the practice of cremation so long as it did not become a public nuisance.—Lord HERSCHELL said the subject was fully discussed in the House of Commons in 1884 or 1885, when it was pro- posed to legislate on the subject —The motion was with- drawn. _
CUSTOMS.—The report of tha amendments to the Cus- toms Consolidation Act (1876) Amendment Bill was read.

THE Thins Bitt.—The Marquis' of SALISBURY, in response to an appeal from the Duke of N'arlborough, postponed the committee stage of the Tithes Rent Charge Bill till Monday week, and took the opportunity of stat• ing that in consequence of a large number of represen. 'tatiobs he had received on the subject he did not propose to insist upon the provision with regard to the 5 per cent. discount The House rose at 7 10. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Ttmsnar.

The Speaker took the chair at 4 p.m. In reply to Sir Thomas Esmonde, Colonel KINO-HARMAN explained that it was reported to the police on April 27th that one of Colonel Rowley's cows, at Rathfarnham, had had its tail cut off, but a police examination disclosed the fact that the loss of the animal's tail was due to dices-se. (Laugtter.) This would not appear in any return of outrages. In reply to Mr. Broadhurst, Mr. STUART WORTLRY Said the Employers' Liability 13111 had been remodelled in many particulars since it was last mentioned in the House. The Home Secretary would introduce the bill on the earliest available opportunity. " In reply to Mr. Buchanan, Sir J. GORST said that in the event of the Duke of Connaught's Leave Bill becom- ing law no additional charge, direct or indirect, would be thrown upon the revenues 0!, India. There would be a saving of the revenue. (Hear, hear.) In answer to Mr. Lawson, Mr. T. NORTHCOTE said the Secretary for War was personally responsible for the delay in the issue of the new, Volunteer regulations. He had kept them back to consider what modifications could be made to meet objections of hon. members, and for the changes made he had also to obtain the sanction of the Treasury.

IRISH MEMBERS AND GOVERNMENT COMMIS.. • • /OS NS. Mr. MoLtoy then read a letter which he addressed to Lord Cross, the Chairman of the Royal Commission on Education, resigning his seat on that body. In this communication the hon. momber stated that self-respect required him to take this course, since he had received his appointment in 1885, when the Conservative party was in close alliance with the Nationalist party, while the members of the Government had recently, for party purposes, assented in reproducing and circulating the scandalous libels of The Times against his colleagneeln the representation of Ireland.—This 'announcement was received with cheers from the Irish members.

Maurice Maly, were previouely inserted in the Bill for the protection of witnesses. Other amendments were rejected by majorities of 68, 30; and 100. The closure had the effect of stopping the discussion of a proposal to leave out Sub-sec- tion 3, which provides that no witness shall be excused from answering questions at preliminary inquiries, on the ground that he may criminate himself, though his answers are not, except in case of indictment for perjury, to be used against Mr. Smith's claim to move the closure had been pre- coded by a warning erieech urging greater deepatch. This elicited a very aegry protest from Mr John, Ellie, who re- sented the language addressed to the House by the gentle- man who "represented the shopkeepers in the Strand." The closure motion was passed by 265 votes to 162, and the words which Mr. Smith proposed to incilde in the Bill ware adopted by 267 to 167. Progress was soon afterwards reported. MrseELIANNons--Mr. FINLAY mays& for permission to bring in a Bill to amend the law as to reForts of proceedings in courts of law, bat Dr. Tanner objected, and the motion could net be propeeed.—Mr. HENRY FOWLER complained that while nearly two months ago a return was ordered with reference to resident magistrates in Ireland, and while a fortnight ago it was used in manuscript, the printed report was not yet in the hands of members. The House adjourned at six o'clock. 1101/8B OF LORDS.—TRIIRSDLY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat shortly after four o'clock.

MISCELIANIIOI7S.—The second reading was moved of a bill to give facilities to farmers to sell their cattle at mar- kets and tairs by weight. The Government accepted the bill, but suggested that the Committee stage should be delayed as loog as possible : Lord Balfour of Burlsigh remarking that a Royal Commission was aboat to be issued to consider the whole question of markets and tolls. It was arranged to delay the Committee stage for some weeks so that the provisions of the measure may be considered by the agricultural world, and the bill was read a second time.
Their Lordships adjourned at fiftem minutes past five o'clock.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.-TIMESDAY.

The Speaker took the chair at QUESTIONS, &C.—Tbe CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER stated that it would be contrary to precedent to make F,ublic the proceedings of the Currency Commission during its sitting, bat it was proposed at an early date to made an Interim report to her Majesty of the proceedings.—Baron DE Womus announced that the inquiry by a Seleet Com- mittee into the loss of life at sea had been extended, and now included almost everything not within the scope of the Royal Commission inquiring into the same subject.— Sir J. Fenoussozr, replying to Mr. Hubbard, said the French Government bad been informed that her Majesty's Government did not propose to take any official part in the Exhibition to be held in Paris in 1889, but would give every facility te persons desirous to exhibit or to contribute to the undertaking._

LORD GRANAR.D'S EVlCTlONS.—Answering an inquiry made by Mr Chance as to the evictions oss Lord Granard's estate, Colonel Kneo-lianarAN read a letter from Lord Granard's agents stating that they had been obliged to press for payment of rents overdue in consequence of baying to meet cash charges on the estate, the chief charge being interest due to the trustees of Maynooth College, which the trestees did not feel justified in allowing to fall into arrears. Lord Granard had stated that he was quite ready to assume the responsibility for the evictions on his estate.—Upon this answer, Mr T Hasty re- marked that he thought the right hon, gentleman would now see that the Maynooth College authorities were in no sense responsible for the action that had been taken Doan or CONNAUGIET'S LIEAVB BILL—The second read- ing of the Duke of Connaught's Leave Bill was moved by Sir J. Goiter, who stated that its object was to give leave of absence to his Royal Highness in order to enable him to re- turn to this country to attend the celebration of the Queen's Jubilee. The bill would not allow his Royal Highness to draw his pay and allowance during his absence.—Mr. Dat,- Nene moved the rejection of the bill, arguing that when these appointments were given to exalted personages it ought to be on the same conditions as applied to other per- sons.—The amendment was seconded by Sir J. SWINBIIIINE. —The bill was read a second time by 318 to 45—A sugges- tion made by Mr. San= that the bill should be at once passed through it. remaining stages 'vas objected to by several members; and Mr. Smith gave notice that he would make a motion on the subject next day. The metion to appoint a Select Committee to inquire into the Army and Navy Estimates was agreed to. POST•OFFICR Paemoteaon.—Mr. CONYBRARR called atten- tion to the question of Post-office patronage, and complained that the beet persons had not been selected. He proposed to move that it is desirable that the present system of pat- ronage, so far as it depends upon party influences, should tease ; but the SPRAKER informed him that he could not move any resolution, inasmuch as no notice of it had been given.—Mr. RAIHRS, in his reply, stated that in the parti- cular case referred te he bad taken the eouree which he be- lieved would be for the best inteeesis of the public Unice. Other grievances were then discussed. Stipptv.—At a quarter to one o'clock the House got into Committee of Supply on the Vote of £17,000 for the prepara- tions at Westminster Abbey for the Jubilee Celebration. The sum, as explained by Mr. Plunket, was made up of £OOOO for the erection of galleries to provide for the ac- commodation of 10,000 persons, £51300 for furnishing, £l3OO to the Dean and Chapter for insurance against damage, and for loss of fees to officials while the Abbey is In possession of the Government, and £llOO for stationery and clerical assistance. Mr. LABoucaurtz moved the redaction of the vote to £2OOO, objecting to the expensive conversion of the Abbey into a " racecourse stand under the auspices of some West-end upholsterer."—The amendment was negatived by 208 to 84, and tbe House adjourned at a qaarter to three.

div.head: CRIMES BILL.
div.p: THE CRIMES BILL.

In Committee on. the Criminal Law Amendment (Ire. land) Bill,, Mr. T. M. Hasty (Longford) moved an amendment providing that every person committed for contempt under the enactments referred to in the clause should be treated as a first-class misdemeanant. The hon. night- ber argued that persons who were merely committed Per contempt in refusing to answer questions ought not to be subjected to the same punishment as was meted Oft to criminals, and stated from the experience of the last Crimes Act that the effect of the mere detention had to many cases been to shorten life by ten years.-41r, '.T. BALFOUR said the Explosives Act eave the poitlef now asked for.—Mr. GLADSTONE called attention to the difference between such examination as the Explosives Act was intended to meet, and the case of a man who was summoned to give evidence as to whether some one had induced somebody else to take, or refuse to take, -a particular farm, or to deal, or refuse . to deal, with some particular tradesman. (Cheers.) Mr. A. J. BALFOUR considered the argument ,of the right hon. gentleman entirely irrelevant. The question was not the difference in gravity of the offence inquired Into, but whether the witnesses were to be compelled to answer the questions put.—Mr. Molloy, Mr. ClanceY, and Mr. Picton, supported the amendment,.-.--Mr. T. M. HEALY put it to the Government whether th;iy would agree that men committed under the clause should not be kept in solitary confineinerft more than 20 hours out of the 24.--Mr. A. J. BALFOUR promised that the Government would look into the mode in which the law was adminlstered, and prevent undue harshness.__. Mr. T. P. O'Conton, referring to the remarks previously made by Mr. Phslay, remarked upon the singularity Of the fact that whenever a Liberal Unionist interfered in the debate it was for the purpose of encouraging the government in brutality. (Cheers from the Irish benches), He denounced the clause as inhuman, and cited dues in which the detention of ,prisoners under the Celine Act had led to insanity and death.—Mr. BUD, i.stiox also spoke in support of the amendment, and gave instances of the serious results that had been , brought about in cases where witnesses had been ins- prisoned for contempt.—Mr. W. H. SMITH appialed to the Committee to permit a division to be taken, and en- dorsed the promise of the Chief Secretary to correct un- due harshness in the administration of the law.—Mr. GLADSTONE repeated the doubt he had expressed as to , the propriety of placing in the same category the man who refused to answer a question about an inducement to refrain from taking a farm, and the person who re- fused iton forward the ends of criminal justice.—The House divided—

For the amendment 144 Against The announcement of the numbers was received with loud Opposition cheers. Mr. T. M. HEALY (Longford) then Moved a proviso limiting the sentence in case t;of infringement of the clause to seven days imprisonment --The ATTORNEY. GENERAL for IRELAELI opposed the amendment, and thought the magistrates might be trusted to administer the law in a fair and just spirit.—Sir W. HARCOURT enlarged On the fact that tinder the clause, as it stood, witnesses at private inquiries before resident magis- trates could be compelled to answer questions, and im- prisoned for refusing to answer questions, as to matters of hearsay, which could not be put under the ordinary rules of evidence.—Mr. 13Aulourr replied that the wit- nesses under the clause were safeguarded to, this extent, that nothing stated them at a preliminary inquiry could be used against them on any other proceedi4.-7, After some further discussion the committee divided— For tho amendment lll Against —The result was received with Opposition cheery.

Mr. M. HEAL! (Cork) moved a proviso that warrants of committal shall specify the offence as tO which the in• quiry has been held, and set forth the question for re, fusing to answer which the witness has been committed to prison, and in the case of ulterior proceedings by such witness the court shall have power to review the whole of the circumstances connected with the committal, and also the order of the magistrate.— The Arroanar- GENEnAL for IRELAND was unable to. accept the amend- ment, though he had no objection to the warrant setting forth the question for refusing to answer which the wit- ness was committed. He had, he said, given notice of an amendment which would meet all that %goes required, but he could not assent to the proposal as to a review of the proceedings of the magistrate, with regard' to which there were already sufficient safeguards by appeal and civil action.—A good deal of discussion followed.--The House divided. For the amendment 155 Against Mr. O'DOHERTY moved an amendment providing that a warrant of arrest should not issue except on a state- ment, made upon oath, that the witness had removed from the jurisdiction of the magistrate, and would not otherwise be forthcoming at the inquiry.—The Ar- roaNer-Gerreest. for lenspre resisted the amendment. —The House divided:— , For the amendment 129 Against Mr. Caexce next moved an amendment, a proviso to the effect that no warrant should be issued for a woman unless after a summons previously served.—Mr. A. J. Betrome opposed the amendment. _ ,• •
The House divided— For the amendment ll7 Against Progress was then reported. The House adjourned at 1 25 a.m.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at twenty minutes past twelve o'clock._

According to the "native source" of Afghan news at Bombay, persistent reports are current that Kleist+ Ghilzai bas fallen, and that the rebels are besieging Ghnznee. The Ameer has sent large reinforcements to the garrison.

-- Nnwes.srn EXHIBITION. The Newcastle Exhibition was opened at noon on Wednesday by the Duke of Cam- bridge, who was accompanied by a number of influential local gentlemen. The Lord Lieutenant of Ireland aad Mr. John Morley took part In the proceedings. The streets were crowded, and the greatest interest was shoyn in the proceedings. His Royal Highness In the afternoon re- viewed the volunteers of the district. To-day he will in- spect the Elswick Works of Sir W. Armstrong and CO. GENERA]. NEWS.

The Wr7entham justices on Menday committed George Moore, a Salvation Army captain, to prison for saran days, for obstructing the public streets. He refused to pay a fine. At West Hartlepool, on Monday, Mr. C. J. Palraer, soli- citor, sena, fined, at the instance of the Tees Salmon Fishery Bbard, £2 for using salmon roe while fishing in Claxton Beek on April Bth, and RI for taking salmon smelt on, that day. _

MURDER BY ' A LUNATIC.—At Stafford Assizes on Mon- day, William Smith, a labourer, was indicted for mur- dering hi& infant grandchild, which had been left in his care by the mother. The prisoner, it was proved, was clearly of unsound mind, and he was ordered into detention as a criminal lunatic Her Ill'ajesty's Government have awarded the silver shipwreck medal to the thirteen men forming the crew of the•Ftench lifeboat of St. Valery-en-Caux, which put out under circumstances ot difficulty and danger to the rescue of two boat's, containing 39, persons, belonging to the steamer Victoria, wrecked near Cape d'Aitty. Messrs. Caird, of Greenock, launched on Monday a new steamer, the Victoria, for the Peninsular and Oriental _

Company. She is 6,600 tons burden, and the largest steamer yet built at Greenock. Her engines are 7,000 nominal horse-power. She has been built to Admiralty requirements, and will be capable of accommodating 2,500 troops. THE CREWE TRAGEDY.—On Monday, Mary Janes, the little girl who was so terribly beaten when her aunt was murdered in Henry-street, Crewe, on the 26th March, was removed to a convalescent home, in North Wales. She is slowly recovering from her injuries. It is not improbable that before the case comes on at the assizes the police will make Another arrest RELATED TO THE QUEEN.—At Windsor, on Saturday, a marrien woman, named Fowler, was charged with being a wandering lunatic. The defendant went to Windsor Castle on Wednesday; and on being asked what she wanted she said she wished to see the Queen, who was her mother's cousin, and that she had an invitation to go to Windsor Castle whenever she liked. The magistrates ordered her removal to the county asylum. SERIOUS RAILWAY ACCIDENT.—On Monday afternoon, a Newcastle passenger train ran violently against the end of the dock at Rattersby Junction, near Middlesbrough. The guard, named Wilkinson, was picked up unconscious on the floor of his van, and was conveyed home with serious injuries to his back, and several ribs broken. Some half-dozen passengers were much shaken and bruised, but were able to proceed on their journey. The train was being shunted at the time of the accident.

Charles Smith, aged 63, a gipsy hawker, was hanged at Oxford, on Monday. for wife murder. While he was being pinioned by Berry, the condemned man sad, You have no need to put those things on me. I will put you to no trouble." When the melancholy proces- sion reached the scaffold, and the executioner was ad- justing the leg straps, the culprit exclaimed. "Oh, dear l" and fainted. The bolt was at once drawn, and, in the opinion of the prison surgeon, death was in- stantaneous. GREAT FIRE AT NorrINCAAf.—A fire of considerable magnitude broke out in aril old quarter of Nottingham on Monday, resulting in, the complete destruction of an extensive timber yarduhelonging to Mr. David Charles Woodhouse. Several: small tenements adjoining were consumed, and a complete panic set in amongst the in- habitants in the neighbourhood, who hastily removed the furniture from their houses, which at one time appeared to be doomed. A man named Martin was very severely burned while rescuing valuable horses from the stables, and remains in a critical condition. A large quantity of machinery was destroyed. A WOMAN'S BIGAMY.—" OUTRAGEOUS PROSECUTION.”— _

At Derby Assizes 024 Monday, before Mr. Justice Hawkins, Mary Ann Riley pleaded guilty to a charge of bigamy at Leicester. The Judge said it was an outrageous prosecution. The prisoner's husband inflicted on her as cruel an outrav as any man could possibly commit. He afterwards deserted her, and she married again, but her second husband also used her cruelly, and arranged with the first husband to bring this prosecution. He could not say she was justified in her conduct, but his con- science would not allow him to send her to gaol. He sentenced her to five Minutes' imprisonment, and she was at once released.

THE BARNSLEY WIFF.-KILIANG CAM—At Leeds Assizes, I on Saturday, Isaac Flazlehurst, a collier, was charged with the murder of his wife on Sunday, March Pith. Prisoner and several companions were dnnking together at the former's house, at Wombwell, near Barnsley, the prisoner's wife joining them. Ultimately she became intoxicated, whereupon prisoner ordered her to bed. Subsequently, while the prisoner went out for more drink, two of the men went upstairs, and on the.prisoner find ma this ou h clfrrect the house. A quarrel fol- • loWed b:eell 1,146,mer his wife., during which the latter received nine wounds Sn the head, sixteen kicks on the lower part of the body, and two broken ribs. The jury returned a verdict of manslaughter, and Ilazle- hurst was sentenced to twelve months' imprisonment. THE AMERICAN EXTEEITION IN LoNnorr.--The Exhibi- tion of Arts and M''''Sctures of the United States at West Brompton was of• on Monday afternoon, in the, presence of a large assemblage of persons. At balf-parlt' three the Grenadiers' Band played "Hail Columbia," after which Archdeacon Farrar led the company in prayer, invoking the blessing of the Almtglity upon the undertaking.—Lord Ronald Gower, on behalf of the English Council, delivered an address of welo.uku3 to th& ' American guests, and expressed a hope that the e.xhibl. tion might be a bond of amity between England and America.—Colonel Henry Russell, president of the exhf., bitien, returned thanks.—After some national songs had euFndered, Colonel Russell started the machinery and prociainlLl en exhibition open. The assembly after- wards proceeded t,;-Vithese the performance of Buffalo. Bill's "Wild West." - I

THE COLONIAL CONEERENCi MENTINGE. .1-o. The Colonial Conference, at its final meeting on Monday, discussed the questions whether colonial governors should be bound to act upon the advice of the Executive Council in Cases of granting or withholding pardons, and granting or refusing dissolution, or whether the existing practice should be maintained. The ques- tion of securing uniformity of returns for the next census was then considered. Sir S. Griffith afterwards briefly summed up the work o't the-Conference and the advantages which had accrued from it, and expressea the confident hope that the results which might be expected to arise from it would tend to strengthen the Nwire id Oraw the colonies more closely together, both with the mother country and each other. Sir Henry Holland expressed his hearty concurrence, and declared the Conference closed. THE POST OFFICE AND MISSING NEWSPAPERS.—Mfe Henniker Heaton, M.P., writes :—"I have to complain of the want of candour on the part of the Post Office re, presentatives. On May 28 of last year I asked the Post- master-General whether he was aware that during the past ten years frequent complaints have been made of the abstraction of large numbers of newspapers sent by people in this country to their relatives and. friends • abroad, particularly in India and Australia. The filtply made in the House of Commons was as follbwn Such complaints have been made on two occasions to the Post Office authorities, but on investigation they have proved to be unfounded.' I myself had made two complaints, and on the following day after the publication of the question I received a sheat of letters endorsing my com- plaint This week the Postmaster-Genoral inform's me that no less than 25,000 newspapers weraposted in England last year for the British colonies, but were not forwarded, in consequence of various irregularities or non-com- pliance with regulations. The mass of these newspapers are sold as waste paper." LONDON CORPIDATION AND TRH Q JEEN.—A pro- cession of carriairs, containing 150 members of the Corporation of London, to Beciiingliam Palace, to present a Jubilee address to the Queen, left the Guildhall shortly after two p.m. on Monday, and proceeded by way of Queen •Victoria-street, Thames Embankment, and Whitehall. At the Palace they were received by the officers of the Royal Household; and were conducted to the picture gallery. whence they were ushered into the i presence of her Majesty in the Throne room. Her Majesty, who was surrounded. by all the great officers of State at the foot of the Throne; replied to the address as follows :—I thank you sincerely for your renewed assur- ance of loyalty and attachment to my Throne and per- son. It gives me great satisfaction, in looking back on the nast history of my. .reign, to recall how much its prosperity is owing, under God, to the sound sense and good feeling of my subjects, and to the sympathy which has united the Throne and the people. I trust that by ! Divine blessing this cordial sympathy may continue un- broken, and that I shall always find, as heretofore, your ancient and illustrious Corporation, in common with all nay other faithful subjects, zealous in every public and private effort to promote the happiness and welfare of the reafra. THE RADCLIFFE MANSLAUGHTER CASE—At the Manchester Assizes, on Saturday, before mr. Justice Wills Thomas Splaine, 35, painter; Norah Splaine, ; /oho 13irch, 30, carter;. and George Kay, 28, dyer; were indicted for having killed and slain Henry Mann, on January 29th, at Radcliffe.—Mr. Blair and Mr. Hamilton were for the prosecution, and Ma Cottingham represented the Splames, and Mr. Mc_Keand was for Birch and Kay. The facts of the case were that about midnight on January 29th a diSturbance too at a lodging-house kept by Birch; between Mrs. = and a man named Roberts. The deceased, Henry Mann, I interfered, whereupon he was dragged into the house and the door was held by someone. Soon afterwards it was discovered that. Mann had received a blow on the head from a poker or some other instrument, and in consegnence of the injuries sustained he died. The evidence was strong that the blow was struck by Theme Splaine, that Birch was behind the door, and that the other prisoners took an active part in the quarrel. Before the case had proceeded far, that against Birch and Kay broke clown, and they were discharged.--For the defence of the Splaines, it was urged that an effort was made to shut the deceased out of the house, but this could not be accomplished. Having got in, it was natural forthe male prisoner to defend his wife. Whilst strugebg getber Mann fell, and his head came in contact with an iron hob.—A verdict of manslaughter was returned, and on Monday the prisoner was sentenced to penal_turvi- tude for seven years.

div.p: CURRENT POLITICS.

IMR. GLADSTONE ON IRELAND. On Wednesday Mr. Gladstoue was entertained at lutcheett by the Rev. Dr. Parker, of the City Temple, London, at his liampetead resideoceorbere the right hon, gentleman met a number of leading Nonconformist minis:era and lay- men. Dr. Parker stated that the company present were de- termined to give Mr. Gladstone every assistance in their power in his resistance to the coercive policy of her Majesty's present advieera. Mr. Gladstone remarked that the year we were passing through, considered as one of the political and legislative life of the nation, was one of posi- tive and absolute retrogression. The free voice of the House of Commons had for the first time been reduced to silence for the purpose of carrying retrogreesiveand repres- sive measures, and the Government had been enabled by the voice of gentlemen who had belonged to the Literal party to appropriate to themselves the time of the House. Allud• log to the relations of the Liberal party to the Nationalists in the House of Commons, the right hon. gentleman justified the grave language he bad used live years agd in reference to the Land League. He cottfd how se- that some of the charges brought against his party by. the Natierialists were true, that the measure for the suspension of the habres cor- pus was unhapoy and mischievous; but they (the Lberalst spoke according to the circumstances that were before them. They spoke the truth then and they spoke the truth now. He asserted that the language used by Celone: Saunderson, Lori' R. Churchill,and Lord Salisbury on the subject of resistance to law in the North of Ireland should Parliament think fit to adopt a measure of Home Rule was language even more dangerous than any ever held by the Irish leaders at the time when their language was de- nounced to the country. But it was a different thing to charge them with complicity with crime. As to the alli- ance between, the Liberals and the Irish party, it was in the pursuit of &coalmen obleet,and must continue until the common object was attained. There was nothing to be ashamed of in such an alliance. Referring to the libels and the refusal of the House Of Commons to deal with them as a breach of privilege or before a Select Committee, Mr Gladstoee said no such butrible farce had ever been enacted in the face of the country as the proposed public proems. tion. Speaking of the Coercion Bill, he Said it was wanton, insidious, dishonouring, and degrading. The die- cushion might be shortened if the Government would say frankly that they would make the bill one against crime only,and not against combination and exclusive dealing, and make it for a limited time, as all other Coercion Bills had been. On the question of Home Rule the right bon gentleman alluded to the report that he was determined to adhere to his plan in all particulars, and said his desire was to see the great object attained which he knew to be essen- tial to the good of the country, and to find the best means of meeting every reasonable objection and of improving the structure of the plan of last year so as to carry with it the greatest possible amount of support. Glaecing at the effect of unduly protracting the present contest, Mr. Gladstone warned his opponents that if they played their rash and ill-considered game too long they would not settle the Irish question upon the easy and favourable terms on which they had still the opportunity of settling it.
Mr. Chamberlain and Mr. Jesse Collings returned to London on Monday after an lbsenee of nearly a mouth.
The Home Secretary reappeared in the House otlanna- mons on .Monctav, but with one of his eyes concealed under a black silk bandage.

At a meeting of the Lancashire and Cheshire Union of Conservative Associations held at Chester on Saturday, Mr. F. S. Powell, M.P., presiding, a resolution was passed expressing confidence in the Government and urging them to pass the Crimes Bill. It is understood that, as the result of Mr. Chamber. lain% visit to the Highlands, a movement is on foot to obtain Liberal Unionist candidates to oppose the Crofter members at the next general election. Afl the Crofter membe—, with the exception of Mr. Fraser Mackintosh, are Gladstonian Liberals.

The Marquis of Hartington, as chairman of the Select Committee on the charges of malversation tit the Lon- don Corporation funds, distributed the draft report of the Committee on Monday. it is understood that the Committee found the allegation. proved, though under condoning circumstances. Sir Thomas Grove, Liberal Unionist member for South Wilts, speaking at Donhead on Saturday night, said that it one thing more cowardly than anotherhad been perpe- trated in this country it WAS the accusations in The Amer. Be believed the Government had made a mat mistake, and done a very stupid action. Mr. Schnadhorst has handed over the £250 contributed by Mr. Chamberlain to the Schnadhonst Testirnonal Fund to the Birmingham Liberal Association. Mr. Chamber- lain's subscription was given before the Home Rule scheme split up the party. Mr. Sehadhorst's step has provoked much comment in political circles. A meeting of the General CO'Uncil representing the Liberal party in the Middleton Division of Lancashire was held at Rochdale on Saturday, when Mr. C. H. Hop-- wood, who was defeated by the present Conservative member, Mr. Thomas Fielden, delivered an address, and was unanimously, adopted as the Liberal candidate for the division at the next eleetion.

BANQUET TO MR. GOSCHEN. e „ A gathering of Unionists, Conservative and Liberal, took place on Saturday night at the Criterion, London, the occasion being a banquet given• to the Chancellor of the Exchequer by his constituents to celebrate his return for the metropolitan division of St. George's, Hanover. square. There were 460 noblemen and gentlemen pre- sent, of whom 340—a large proportion M.P.'s—found places in the great hall of the establishment, u der the presidency of the Prime Minister, the remainder having to be accommodated in the eastern annexe, which.com- enunicates with the pripcipal apartment Among those present were the Duke of Abercorn, the Duke of Leeds, the Duke of Westminster, the Earl of Dunraven, the Earl of Harrowby, the Earl of Arran, the Earl of Galloway, Earl Bathurst, the Earl of Erne, the Earl of Fowls, the Earl of Northbrook, the Earl of Beehive, the Marquis of Lothian, ~ the Marquee of Abergavenny, the Marquis of Hertford, ''' ' FOOTBALL. the Marquis of, Ormonde, Lord Rowton, Lord Lorides-.: borough, Lord Henry Bruce, Lord Stalbridge, Lord Elcho, FINAL TIE OF THE VALOR COMPETITION. the Lord Chancellor, Viscount Sidmouth, Viscount WARRINGTOII,2ND v.
