If the Church is in Ihe A e chains be removed • hat let it ekt„, uee, -Alen of ot.Y and in order by the formal Church and State. 1,4 ,t th th:/tk eeouktloothly Meeting of the Warrington 1111114uptio,scil, on Tuesday, the question of ltsett_u• of the Report of the Library he Report has reference to t),topcatiett. "I... Committee came under con- , ,414 .talt 1 '44t'tillittrarcualeph have been male for making ree Lending Library, and is t° 2tePS being taken under present

circumstances to make the Library free as part of the Tubilee celebration. Councillor DIXON moved, and Councillor H. ROBERTS seconded, that the minutes of the Library and 1 Museum Committee be confirmed with the exception of the Report on the question of freeing the Library, and urged that it was desirable that the matter should not be closed until further measures had been taken to meet the difficulties of the situation. It was explained by the TOWN CLERK that there I was no question of the adoption of the Report —it was simply laid before the Council; and the MAVOR and Alderman WEama taking the same view, and urging that the question would be still an open one, the amendment to the minutes was withdrawn. In the course: of the•discussion, the MAYOR 'intimated that, he had "received suggestions that morning 'front Mr. TIMIAS MORRIS, which he con- sidered rather favourable to the Free Lending Library movement ;" but it-did not transpire 'what these suggestions were until Councillor FL ROBBRITS explained that he had reason to believe thEt Mr. MORRIS, or someone in his behalf, was prepared to deposit Corporation bonds to the amount (it £5OO to be drawn upon tomake good any deficiency from sub- scriptions that might arise during the next five years. The MAYOR Temarked as to this that it was" a very fair offer ;" and we are disposed to think the public will echo the observation. For our part we regard it as exceedingly if not unnecessarily generous. The subscribers have no locus slam& in law; there is not a single clause in any one of the Acts of Parliament relating to Free Libraries which makes reference to them; and we have no hesitation in saying that it is absolutely illegal tevive them anyjprivileges which ore not shared ley the rest of the ratepa_yers. And yet it is because of the subscriptions and the fear of their falling off that the Library Committee refuse to do that which they. ought to have done 30 years ago, namely, make the Library a Free Lending Library! But Mr. MORRIS has taken the bull by the horns, and, if we are not greatly mistaken, he will lay it on its back. That there may be no misapprehen- sion as to his meaning, we give his proposal for making the Library free as it was submit- ted to the MAYOR. It is as follows :

That the institution be carrie&on on the same lines and in all respects as it now is, with the addition that any ratepayer wanting a book, without paying a subscription, shall sign a voucher of responsi- bility; also get his reader's ticket signed by two well-known ratepayers, similar to what is done in all Free Leading Libraries. CM condition that the above two suggestions are agreed to by the Museum and Library Committee, I will find a friend who will place, In the hands of the Mayor, Warrington Corporation Bonds to the amount of .£5OO, to be drawn upori to make good any deficiency through subscriptions falling off dtiring the next five years. In face of this definite proposal to meet the financial difficulty—a difficulty which is more imaginary than real—we do not see how the Library and Museum Committee can raise any objection to complying with the demands of the ratepayers, and going forward in the right path by making the Library free. If they still.continue to block the way, the bar- gesses will know what to think of them, and they will' know how to concert measures for ensuring that the present members of the Committee shall be relieved of their respousi- bilities after the next municipal election. It may be. ,as the Tows CLERK says, that the Town Council have no jurisdiction over the Library Committee after it is appointed; but, happily, it is appointed for one year only.; and, if the present Committee cannot see their way in this matter, it will be quite within the province—indeed it will be the duty of the Town Council, in November next, to elect a Committee more in harmony with the progressive spirit of the age, and at the-same time pledged to carry out the wishes of the ratepayers in the management of a ratepayers' institution.

THE'neW Temperance organisation known as the Warrington Temperance Federation held its-inaugural meeting, on Monday even- ing, in the Public Hall, when there was an attendance which • sufficiently betokened the interest which the masses take in the temper- ance movement. -Speaking of them as a whole, there is good reason to believe that the people are far ahead of their leaders in the desire for legislation on the liquor traffic. , It is certainly the case so far as Warrington is concerned 'Both parties have hitherto fought, shy ofit at Parliamentary elections. 'So lar as the Tories are concerned, it is a matter of Course that this should be so, having a brewer for their-candidate ;'tot it is just because there is a 'brewer in the 'field that the Liberals shoulerbring the question of licensing reform to thefront, by way of showing that .a licen- sing monopolise is the last person to be thought of to represent the people.. As the Rev. Canon LEIGH said at the meeting, there is far too much half-heartedness on the question. The hosts want leading, for,-some- how, when the hour of conflict comes, the leaders are novthere to be found. If the men who stood on the. platform in the Public Hall on Monday would be true to the Federation which they have formed—if they would stand by each other at the next election and -say— "We will neither vote, nor advise out friends to vote, for a candidate /who does not give distinct pledges ow, the temperance question," it is not -too much to say they would have it all their.own way in settling who should 're- present them in Parliament. Let us hope that the formation of this Temperance Federation is the 'inauguration of a *new departure— however much of a reproachit may be to say' that it is new. There are come signs ,that` the clergymen of the Church of England ate resolved to take a firm stand nn the question, and that they will for 'the future be proof at election time against the blandishments of brewers. it is hard, ne doubt, to turn round on the man who has giuen a fraction of his al-gotten gains in support of the Church and of the school; but it is good for the soul when temptation comes to be zble to rise to the occasion and say—" Get ti.hee behind me, Satan." Warrington stands greatly in need of temperance men who will mot flinch. It is overshadowed by great brewers, and is drialt-ridden to an extent which is discredit- able to the whole community. Tisere has been sufficient of preaching; Jet there be something of practice. The Warrington Temperance Federation has set itself a great work; and we trust it will be equal to the task.

THE QUEEN AND THE LIVERPOOL EXEC TBITION.— Her Majesty has, through Sir Henry Posasonby, communicated to the Executive of the Royal Jubilee Exhibition, her wish that the exhibition ahould be opened in her Majesty's name and by her express command, It is considered that the open- ing ceremony, which will be on a scale of great magnificence will in itself be the most appropriate local celebration of the Jubilee. The magnificent Lon- desborough collection of relics of wars, and royal mementoes of all ages hag arrived at the exhibition, i and s being arranged by a representative of Lord Londesborough. Madame Marie Roae will sing the solo part of the National Anthem at the opening ceremony on Monday next. .

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAT 14, 1887.
"TOUCH AND GO."

The Mly Queen was crowned at Golborne art Saturday. If there wasn't much May blossom, there was plenty of May sunshine, and "'her Majesty's" subjects seem to have had a happy time of it. This year, Miss Frances Clynes was the "Queen rose bud of the garden of girls."

Lolt,cl Salisbury, in answer to a question in the House of Lords on Tuesday night, said the practice of cremation had not become sufficiently common to call for Parliamentary interference. It is lawful; a man may not merry his grandmother, but he may cremate her,

The agriculturist is wide awake; the pinch 'of poverty has sharpened his wits, and given him eyes all round. On Monday, there was a pubic Conference, in London, of the Farmers' Alliance, at which the weak points of Lord Salisbury's Tithes Bill were mercilessly ex- posed. The farmers will have none of it; they are not disposed to grasp at a shadow.

The latest novelty in the way of Jubilee celebration comes from Backbarrow, in the Furness district, where the inhabitants are erecting a building to be called The Jubilee Lockup." If some other Barrow, back or front, would only top this by erecting a Jubilee Asylum for all who are Jubilee mad, it might be said that the fitness of things was perfect.

Aldeiman Crosfield may well question the statement as to the average illuminating power of Warrington gas being equal to 18 candles at both works. It is sometimes so low as to illumination as to sqt one thinking that one candle would hold its own against the vas. Printers make remarks when they are left to grope for small type which they cannot see, and they are not remarks that smooth the way to the better land.

And then there is the question of charges. Some famous charges were made at the battle of Waterloo, but compared with those of the Gas Department of the Warrington Corpora- tion they are behind thv record. When complaint is made, Town Councillors laugh —Mr. Tinsley knows how they laugh—and there the matter ends. There is an increase in the gas bill at our own works of from 35 to +o per cent. We can pay, and, of course, grumble. Will somebody else thus treated give us their experience?

"The Home Secretary has agreed, it is stated, to receive a deputation, on Tuesday next, to protest against the proposal con- tained in the amendments to the Mines Re- gulation Bill to prevent women working at the pit's brow." Just so : Acts to prevent women working under ground are well enough ; but to say they shall not work above grouxd—at the pit mouth—is going too far. " Men, my brothers," this will never do ; it is not kindly; it is oppressive.

The Rev. Canon Leigh, at the Temperance Meeting, on Monday, observed that it had been said the reason why so many brewers were 'millionaries was "because for one man who has brains there are thirty who have stomachs:" Granted, but there is another 1 reason—it is because the brewer has ob- tained, through his licences, a monopoly to profit by the degradation of his fellow-men. l'Some day the brewer will have the impudence to ask for compensation for interference with his monopoly.; he will want paying a second time for having brought a curse on the com- munity. John Bull would .do well, mean- while, to think this matter. over. -- -Mr. Smith seems to have thought in the matter of the closure it was -simply a case of " ask and have;" but he was undeceived on Tuesday morning. Yfr. Courtney as the Chairman of Committees refused to apply the gag in the wholesale fashion in which it was demanded. Mr. Smith is not a heaven-born Minister.; heis Mr. Smith—very good as an agent'for the sale of newspapers; very poen- as a leader of the House of Commons.

The present House of Commons is incap- able of dealing justly with Ireland, or with Irishmen. The rejection, on Saturday morning, of Mr. Gladstone's proposal to grant a Select Committee to inquire into the foul charges of the "Times" as to " Far- nellism and crime'' is an appalling revelation of the blinding 'influence of party prejudice. It is but fair to acknowledge that the chief Conservative organ, the -" Standard," re- fused to defend the indefensible. How could it, when it advised that the scope of the 'inquiry should be widened, and this was done'?

Mr. Labouchere.ruade a racy and power- ful speech. In the course of it he said : " Theirich members had good authority and good precedence ifor treating 'with contempt the outpourings of the Times,' for that ,newspaper had attacked Mr. Cobden and Mr. Bright in s. series of mcst atrocious articles. (Cheers.) Mr. Cobden had written to the editor of the ' Times' asking,•' Is it seriously contended that as often as you choose to.pre- vert the sense of our,speeches and to charge us with a scheme of public robbery, the onus lies with us‘to disprove the imputation, and that we have no right to complain if we do not do so that we are henceforth tobe treated as rokbersr" There is no answer to this, and it puts the whole case in a nutshell.

The Government were in the position, in suggesting a reference to the Law C4surts, of challenging an opponent to fight a duel with a weapon which they 'icnew that opponent mould clot accept. How gallant! They would not say a breach of Iprivilege had been ,committed ; or that it Lad ,not been com- rritted 4hey would not say anything. What bravery! Hencecorth it -is understood that when the -Tories are in power the House of Commons is not guardian of its own honour; ,it has no hcnour to guard.

jgdge Ffoulkes has no sympathy with eg- actions for mon-paryment of instalments which are sometimes enforced in connection with agreemenis for goods oliitained on the hire system. Dealing with some cases brought into the Runcorn County Court, on Tuesday, he said the tennis sought to be en- forced were oppressive, and refused to make orddars for charges for failure to pay within the specified time. His Honour showed himself to be the guardian of the poor, re- cognizing that it is the function of the law to protect the weak against the strong.

THE MITTMAN. OUTBREAK IN CELESHIRE.—Messrs, pereivai, farmers, of Aston, upon whose premises serious outbreaks of disease have occurred among turn stock, having applied to the Privy Council for compensation for the destruction of 87 pigs, have received a letter stating that the animals were not ordered to be slaughtered, and therefore the Privy Council have no power to award any com- pensation. LOCAL PATENTERS.—The following local patents have lately been sealed :-‘4,199 (of 1866 ) John Brock, Widr es, Lancashire and Thomas Minton, Widgets, for " Improve- ments in the manufacture of bleaching powder, and in ap- paratus for effecting the same." 6,013 (188t3.) SIMMS'S CROSS PRIMITIvH METHOOST SUNDAY SCHOOL. —The anniversere services in aid of this echool were held on Sunday, when the Rev F Shirnmin preached morning and evening to good congregations. In the afternoon the service of song entitkd " Joseph" was rendered by the choir and a few friends Mr. James Hargreaves presided, and there was a good attendance. The collections realistd a satisfactory sum. PROPERTY IN THE MARKET AT WIDNES.— Mr. Barnett Dutton, auctioneer, Oakland-street, has offered for sale by public auction a small lot of property consisting of shop and house and private house situate in Oekland•street, There were numerous bids, but the reserve was not reached, and the property Has withdrawn. It is expected that the ' property, which was offered by the executors of the late Mr. Edward Tickle, will be disposed of by private treaty. RUNCORN Buaret. BOARD.—The monthly meeting was held on Wednesday, at the cemetery office. Mr. Littler presided, and there were present Messrs. Morris, Colebure,l and W. F. Salkeld (secretary). It was report.d that during the month ended April 25th there were 20 interment., an increase of two upon the correspondisg period of last year. The fees received during the same period amounted to £22 15s 6d, an increase ef Li us 6d on last year. There was no other business of public interest. EXCITING!. STRUGGLE AT WES‘7OII POINT.--At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mc J. Brundrit and Cap- tain C. W. Herlehurst, a rotigh-looking man, named John Hoek, who was employed as a horse driver along the river Weaver Canal,was charged with aseaulting P.C. Dale whilst in the execution.of his duty. From the statement of the conshiale, it appeared that'on Saturday night he was on duty at:Weston PointfDocks. About eleven o'clock the prisoner, who was drunk, came up to the constable and, using some violent language.atruck him on the breast with his fist, 1 Tien tearing open the constable's coat, the prisoner seized the chain attached to his whistle, and broke it into three pieces. The prisoner followed this up by kicking and strik- lag the constable several times, and the latter now used his stick in self-defence and closed on his assailant. An excit- ing struggle now took place on the ground, the prisoner , calling out to a companion nameel Michael Gibbons to come to hts aid an help him to throw Dale Into the dock. Gib- bons, however, did not respond to the appeal, and Dale being a big powerfol fellow, got the upper hand after a struggle lasting half an hour.—Richard Shaw, the lock keeper, said the constable was more patient with the prisoner than he should have been, and only used his stick in self defence.— I The prisoner alleged that the constable was the aggressor, and said he was smothered with blood from a wound on the bead inflicted by the constable's stick.—Superintendent Hollingsworth said the prisoner bad been living at Barnton, and it was a long time since he was before the Runcorn bench. He mast ask the magistrates to protect the con- , stable in such a dangerous place as Weston Point —Mr. Brundrit said there was no doubt that policemen sometimes exceeded their duty, but there was not the slightest evi- dence in this case. The prisoner was certainly to blame, and they would make an example of him. The prisoner was , sentenced to two months' hard labour.

WIDNES FREE PUBLIC LIBRARY.—The Widnes Free • Library will be thrown open to the public on Monday next. The opening ceremony, which will be of a most unosten- tatious character, will be performed by Professor Rendall, : of the Liverpool University College. At half-past seven the : members of the Library Committee, of the Local Board, and of the School Board, with the medical gentlemen, clergy- , men. solicitors, and other gentlemen in the town will I assemble at, Alforde Chambers at half-past seven They will accompany Professor Randall to the Library Buildings, where the Professor will be presented with a silver key as al memento of the occasion, and he will then open the door. , An inspection of the Library and reading-room will follow, ' and their adjournment is to be 'made to the Baths where Professor Rendall will deliver an address. Tickets for I his 1 meeting may be obtained from Miss Procter at the reading- I room. TRAVELLING WITHOUT A TICKET AT WIDNES —On . Thursday, at Widnea I'etty Sessions, William Ellis, a labourer' was summoned for having, on the Bth April, travelled on the Sheffield and Midland Railway Company. between Garston and Widnes. without having paid his fare, and with intent to avoid payment.—Mr. Whitelegge (Messrs. Bede and Co., Birmingham) prosecuted on behalf of the railway company, and Mr. T. J. Peters defended.— From the evidence of David Forshaw, inspector at Widnes, and George Partington, the booking clerk, it appeared that the defendant alighted from a third-class carriage on the train arriving in Vt'idnes from Liverpool at 9 12 p m. on the evening of Good Friday. He scaled the wooden palings that bounded one side of the station, and dropped to the ground on the other side, a distance of 10 feet. It was dark at the time, and when the officials searched for him they were unable to discover him.--Mr. Peters stated in ex- tenuation of the offence that the defendant did not know what he was doing.—A floe of 5s and costs, 12s, was im- posed. : BREACH OF LICENSE.—AI Widnes Petty Sessions, on : Thursday, Mary Ann Rock, oyster dealer, Widnes•road, was : charged with keeping open her house for the sale of refresh- : ments during the time it ought to be closed. P.C. Forster deposed that at 10-25 on Surid,y night, the let May, he saw several young men enter the defendant's oyster shop. He , went to the door after they had entered and found that it I wee locked. Through the window he saw the defendant I opening oysters for the young men. He then tried to enter I the shop, and the defendant's girl came to the docd., and on I learning who was there she took the plates and other things I from the counter. The door was then opened. Previous e to that the constable lied seen one of the young men hand ; same money to the defendant. Mrs Rock said the did not t know what time it was, and she had received no money.— r Inspr cot Wood said he had cautioned defendant not to I keep her shop open after ten o'clock, and she had stated that she would keep her shop open in spite either of bim or the magistrates.—The defendant, who aolo said she would r get a license, was fined 10s, and costs 12s. 1 STOCKPORT AND THE SHIP CANAL SCHEME. I The Manchester Ship Canal scheme has been taken , up with enthusiasm in Stockport. It was hoped 1 when some of the directors visited the town a few 1 weeks since that £lOO,OOO would be raised, but I nearly 20,000 over that amount is already represen- I ted by the shares taken up. There were also present the Rev. J. J. Lockwood, , Messrs. Mclntyre, Brandreth, Aaron, Lewis, Had- field.Wallington, Knowles, William Whitlow, Smith, H. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy I clerk). There was no business of public interest. I THE LATE M. PETER RYLA.NDS, M.P. There ' has been erected in Thelwall Churchyard a memo- rial stone to the late Mr. Peter Rylands, M.P., executed out of the celebrated green Swedish granite. It bears the following inscription in gold , letters:—" In loving memory of Peter Rylands, born January 18th, 1820, died February Bth, 1887. 'After 'Labour, Rest.' Matt. xi. 28." The memo- rial has been excellently executed by the firm of Messrs. Essenhigh Bros.. sculptors, Manchester- road, Warrington, who have a growing reputation for Vie display of artistic skill in work of this ! description. . I BOWLING Miarn OR £lo.—Joseph Holbrook land James Shaw, two well-known opponents, met lon the Kin.' and Queen Inn bowling green, Pad- gate, on Saturday afternoon, and contested a game .of bowls, 51 up, for ..E5 aside. Upwards of 300 , :spectators surrounded the green, which was in , Igoe(' order, and a well-played and exciting gaime I was expected to be witnessed, as this was the I sixth time the pair had opposed each other in ' 'similar matches. On four occasions, singular to state, the stake at issue had depended on the last ' end; but on Saturday, although the pair kept close together in the first part of the game, their play throughout was only of a second rate character, Holbrook eventually winning by 10 points. PRESENTATION. TO COLONEL MCCORQUODALE. —On Tuesday Colonel McCorquodale. of the Wil- lows, Newton-le-Willows, attained his 70th birth- day. In order to commemorate this epoch in his life, and to give evidence of the high regard in which he is held by his numerous business staff in the firms of McCorquodsle and Co., Limited, and the Liverpool Printing and Stationery Co., of which companies he is chairman, they unitedly presented to him a chiming clock, an elegant model of a stag (his crest) in silver, and an illuminated ad- dress, the value of the whole being nearly £2OO. It must be pleasant for Colonel McCorquodale, who is held in high esteem as a citizen and a magistrate, to find that he has such a 'warm place in the affec- tions of his workpeople. We 'wish him "many happy returns of the day." THE MANCHESTER ROYA.L JUBILEE EXHIBITION. —The admissions to the Jubilee Exhibition on Thursday exceeded 20;000. The grounds were de- lightful in the evenine, and were well filled up to shortly after nine o'clock, when a shower dispersed those who had gathered around the fairy fountains to see and admire their wonderful colours. The apparently endless and almost overwhelming charms aud attractions that meet one on every hand, whether inside or outside the exhibition, elicit the wonder and admiration of every new coiner, and even those who pay a daily visit find on each occasion something fresh to delight the eye or interest the mind. Taking into consideration' the large number of season tickets sold, and the great crowds of visitors who flock their day after day, the popularity of the Exhibition may be re- garded as fully assured. ELOPEMENT FROM DITTON.—The village of Dit- ton has been thrown into a state of excitement by the elopement of a woman of about thirty summers and the mother of three children, with a swain of rather prepossessing appearance. Not very long ago, a workman came to reside at Ditton. where he ' had obtained work at the Liver Chemical Company's works. Soon afterwards a young man came to work at the same place, and took lodgings with the man and his wife. Though the husband on more than one occasion had cause to turn the lodger out, he saw no cause to suspect that there was anything improper in the relations between the lodger and his wife until Saturday last, when, on coming home from work, he found his wife, the younger child, and the lodger missing. Instituting inquiries, he traced them to Liverpool, whence it was found the couple had embarked for America the same day.

The annual general meeting of the members of the With I nes Fostball Club was held at the Central Hotel, Widnes, on Wednesday evening. Dr. Richards presided, and there-was an unusually large number of persons present. The Chairman expressed his pleasure at presiding. and said he was especially pleased as he believed that was one of the best attended football meetings that had ever been held in Widnes, and he thought it @hewed very well for the future prosperity of the club., (Hear. hear.) In reviewing the season they could not take a great deal of credit to themselves, although they could say that they had never been badly beaten during the whole season. (Hear, hear.) It had been said—bat he did not know how true it was— that they had often been beaten by the referee; but in any case tte points against them bad never been very great, and, taking them all in all, it showed that they had not deteriorated in any way—on the contrary, he thought they had improved very much. From the increased interest which had been taken in the game during the last winter, be considered it augured well for the future ; and he thought that if they only tried, bad a little more practice, I and could induce their men to turn up at their matches from home it weld be better. They could always turn up at home, and they could nearly always win at home. (Hear, hear) beveral of their supporters said that they could newer win a match away from home. He ebeuld not like it to ija said for the credit o f Widnes players that it was for want of pluck or want of energy; but it would appear very muck as if ti.cy lost heart when they went away. He, however, hoped and trusted that in the coming season they would show that they could not only play at home but away also. (Hear, bear, and applause.) There "A " team wee undoubtedly much stronger in comparison than their Ere: team. (Applause.) He thought—but he did not know whether it was right—they were capable of tackling anei beating any "A " team in Lancashire. (Applause.) They had been beaten, however, twice, he believed, during the season, by Mossley. The Secretary's report was then read. The results of last season have appeared in this journal The financial report, which was read by the treagurer (Mr J Ashall), showed that the receipts baJ been £373 12s BJ, and the expenditure £347 17s 714, leaving a balance in hand of £25 15s Old. _ . ,The month', meeting was held at Alforde Ctiambers on Tuesday. Mr. F. H. Gossage, J.P., presided, and there were present—. Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. H. Gaskell, junior, J P., E. Carey, T. Handley, D. Wright, J. Midwood, J. Taylor, J. Houghton, 8. Sadler, B. Brown, F. Heyes, R. Cook, J. T. Allen (clerk), 1. Carr (gas engineer), W. Higginson (stir. veyor), J. Dickson (nuisance inspector).

Each rod weighed about 4 cwt. and had to be hoisted 130 feet. The method by which the rods were raised was as follows :—A travelling crane, which was worked by manual labour, occupied a nos tion 21 feet above the mouth ef the well. This crane was the property of the , Local Board, and had been in use for about 12 years. The man to look after the crane when it got wrong would be Helsby, the foreman fitter. There was a platform round the crane of a 13 inch plank. At each corner ef ' this platform was an upright, with lin. gas pipio4 fixed in ass protecting rail. When he saw the machine after the acci- dent one of the handles was off the crane, and one of the rails was out. There had been twe or three " n irrow chances" with the crane. The rail had come out, but they had had to press heavily to get it out. The rail could be made a great deal better by being bolted to the upright. He had no fault to find with the fastening of the handle to the crane.—A juryman said the rail round the platform had been more of a decoy than a protection—Witness: Yes.— In answer to questions, witness said he had often remarked that it was not safe, and he had thought he would name the matter to Mr Carr, but it had always slipped cut of his mind. If the rail had been fast he did not think his son would have fallen down.—Mr Carr informed the jury that at the time of the accident the deceased was in the employ of Meant+ Hawthorne, Davies, and Co., contractors. He proceeded to question the witnese, who said he had never teld Mr Carr tliatthe platform was 'unsafe, and did not know that he kn, w. The rail was safe enough to walk along by, and wanttit a cossiderable press to loosen it.—Tbomas Houghton, a young loan, said the deceased was his brother; His brother was &Sten in the well with Helsby and another man, and he and a man named Manifold were working the crane. ,About half-p.st.twelve he and Manifold were trying to get the crane from double gearing to single gearing, and Heleby, who heard them, sea the deceased who knew more abouethe maChine te help them. His bro.. ther, when he got upon the platform, got bold of one of the handles of the crane and pulled strongly. The handle came off, and he went crash against the handrail, which gave IVAV. and he fell to the ground clutching at the stage as he descended. The handle that his brother had hold of was not fastened with a nut. He (witness) had taken it off, to Chance the handles, and he bad not ecreaved It on again.— ' The Coroner: If you had put the nut on the handle again, this woald not have happened, would it ?—Witness: I don't ;.suppose it wool], sir—By Mr. Carr: lie would have con- Libidered it unsafe to pull at the handle without the not, but 'his brother was in such a hurry they could not tell him anything. He did not consider the handrail of the stage safe. If it had been firm his brother would have been saved.—Peter Manifold, labourer, gave evidence of a con- firmatory character.—Mr. Carr explained that the pipes had been fastened in the uprights by " swelling," bat by con- stant usage it must have become insufficiently firin to resin the force of a body coming against it.—A. Jourym tn con- tended that that was a bad principle of fixing the pipes.— The Coroner in snniming up,sald it must be admitted that the primary cause of the aCcid4nt lay with the brother, be- cause if he had screwed on the nut that he had palled off most probably the accident would not have happened. At the same time the evidence disclosed that the handrail of the platform' was not in a secure condition ; and it seemed to him-that a crane working 21 feet from the ground should be protected in the best manner possible.—After about ten minutes liberation. ,the jury returned a verdict of acci- dental death, and added a presentment that the present platform is in a' very dangerous condition and quite insuffi- cient for the work uporrit. They suggested that a new platform be erected not less -than 2 net wide, with proper fencing around it.-r The Coroner: I think it a very proper verdict and a very proper presentment.

RUNCORN FOOTBXLL • CLUB:—ANNUAL MEETING!' The annual meeting of the members of this club was bed in the large room of Wilson's Hotel bn'Weonesdav There was a capital attendance, 'and Mr. J. R. Frith sided.

The Chairman remarked that this was a meeting purely for business, and he did not propose to make any lengthy observations. He must say how very mach pleased he was with the progress which had been made during the past year. He made the remark to a Liverpool player of some note a short time ago, that he little thought that Runarn would be so conspicuotts in the football world in so short a time. (Hear, hear.) He made this, to him very pleasing, reply : That it was because the Runcorn players had played a good'gentiemanly game that they bad risen in the estitna- ation, and had worked their way up as they had dOne. He congratulated himself and congratulated everybody round upon the success attained—(applause)—and he hoped this was only the beginning of some very successful years in the future. (Applause.) Mr. Longshaw presented a report of the past seaion, which he said Vas the most successful one in the annals' of the club. Thirtrthree matches were played, out of which 26 were woo, 3 drawn, and 4 lost, the total score being 33 goals, 64 tries, 123 minor points, against their opponents' score of 8 goals, 20 tries, 74 minors. This was no mean majority, considering the class of clubs which were met during the 'eaten. Mr. Longshaw accorded well deserved praise to the members of the first team for the manner in which they had turned up, and said the heartiness which had characterised their play all through the season has been a pleasure to all concerned. Their conduct on the field had been most exemplary. He hoped that when another season had arrived the team tbat had done so well during the year would again don the "green" jersey, and that the same success would follow them. The fixtures arranged for next year were Rochdale Hornets, Salford, Swinton, New Brighton, Manningham' Dewsbury, Birkenhead Park, Broughton Ringers, Oldbam,Barrow,Ken- dal Hornets, Liverpool, Liverpool ota• .ffoys, Manchester Ranger, and Eccles. The lattbr club are given dates when the Cheshire County are playing in Cheshire. It was yet ex- pected to have the offer of dates from the Bradford Club. There' had been pressing offers from Swansea, Llanelly, Add Cardiff.'but the Committee thought it was rather too Fe pensive to travel down to South Waifs. The second team had played 23 matches, 15 being won, 4 lost, and 4 drawn. They scored 30 goals, 43 tries, 92 minor points, against their opponents 3 goals, 8 tries. 32 minor points, giving ' the Runcorn team a Majority of 27 goals, 35 tries, and 60 minor points. The aggregatescore of both first and second 'teams was 63 goals, 107 tries. 215 minors, to their oppo- 'nen& 11 goals, 28 tries, and 106 •ntnors.: Mr. C. WIFE Assaum—Thomas—Ruiling-ten, a respectably- dressed man, was brought up under warrant on a charge of having assaulted his wife on the 11th May.. Complainant, whose face was disfigured, described the assault, and said that her husband had behaved very badly to her of late. She wished to have a separation order, if that could not be granted, she did not want her husband to ge to prison. Pri- soner was ordered to be bound over in his own recognisance' to keep the peace for six months, and also to pa v lOs 6d costs.

A WOMAN'S QUARREL.— Sarah Massey was summoned for assaulting Elizabeth Ashton, and Susan Lee, Annie Leo- nard, and Elizabeth Ashton were summoned for assaulting Sarah Massey. Mr. A. Browne appeared for Massey. The evidence went to show that a general row had taken place in Lord Nelson-street. The Bench came to the conclusion that there had been some hard swearing, and ordered that each of the parties be bound over to keep the peace. MISCELLANEOUS —Joseph Ashton, who did not appear, was fined 5s and costs for striking John Evans on the mouth; and John Kane, charged with assaulting Kate Melior, on the 7th mat, was dismissed.

RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Mr. J. Brundrit and Captain Haslehurst. Dam{ AND DISORDERLY.—For being drunk in Canal. street, on the 10th January, William Disley, a boatman, was fined Z. and costs, Pe 6d.—Emma Meek, of Nelson-square, was charged with committing a broach of the peace in High- street, on the sth May, and on the evidence of P.C. Mil- lington, she was bound over to be of good behaviour for six months in her own recognisance' of 1.5. ALLEGED DAMAGE AT Itlsurom —Charles Thomason, a youth, was charged with having, ea the 22nd April, and Edward Fowler, a youth, with having, on the 3rd May, damaged a wooden fence belonging to Thomas Beach, chemical labourer, of Wooers-row, Malten-lane.—The father of Thomason having apologised, and the youth having promised not to offend again, tbe summons against him was withdrawn. The complainant stated that the boys of the neighbourhood were in the habit of playieg football on a piece of around adjoining his field, and be bad suffered much damage at ',SMOGS times. Oa the 3rd May the ball went into the field, and the defendaat Fowbr scaled the rails, and trespassed upon the fields. The complainant could I.not prove any damage, and the Bench discharged the defen- dant with a caution.

• WIDNES POLICE COURT. MONDAY—Before Mr. I'. S. Timm's. Datiwit awn Disononatv.—Edward Plant, a labourer, was charged with having been drunk in Warrington-road on Saturday afternoon, aod also with having damaged the cell in which he was confined at the Police Station, to the extent of 46d. Inspector Wood and P.S. Clarkson proved the case, and the defendant was ordered to pay 22s 61, or fp) to gaol for 14 days,—John Riley and James Mullen were each fined Se and costs for drunkenness.—James Fleming and Michael McCormick, youths, were ears) bound over to karts the peace for two months for creating a disturbance in Water-street on Saturday night.

,• WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. THORSDAY.—Before Mr. F. 11, Gossage and Mr. George Pilkington. Dltureg atm DISORDERLY —The following persons were each fined for drunkenness :—NfariDaley. Nelson-street, and Jane Jones, Barn-street. Bridget Oates, who bad been 24 times previously convicted, was sent to gaol for a month. Mark O'Brien, Thomas Smith, and John Riley were charged with committing a breach of the peace by fighting in Sat- ton's-lane. P.C.'s Brown and Thompson proved the case, and the defeudants were each bound over to be of good beha- viour for a month. "A LONG Tars Now."—Edward Mulvey was charged with being drunk whilst in charge of a horse and trap in Victoria-road—P.C. Forster having proved the case, the de- fendant said it was 'the first time this 30 years." A fine of 53 and cords. _ . _
DISMISSED.—George Ball was charged with assaulting Mary Boyle irt Eleanor-street, on the 7th May. After hearing the evidance the Bench dismissed the case.

div.head: CHAIRMAN.
div.p: THE CHAIRMAN.

In opening the proceedings the Chairman said the mem- bers were good enough to again appoint him chairman of the Board. He could only say that after so long a service in the position he thanked them for this renewed proof of their confidence. He should be glad to do all he could for the interests of the Board. (Applause).
FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE.

On the proposition of Dr. O'Keefe, seconded by Mr. Handley, the suggestion of the Free Library Committee that Messre. F. H. Pankhurst, J. Fitzpatrick, and W. Sadler be members of that body was adopted. THE INFECTIOUS DISEASES HOSPITAL.

The Clerk read a fetter front the Local Government Board sanctioning the borrowing of £5OO for the purpose of erecting a caretakers cottage to the Infectious Diseases Hos- pital—AL a later period of the proceedings it was decided that the tender of John Bothwell of £543 for the erection of the house be accepted subject to the usual contract and bond.

div.head: BYE LAWS.
div.p: THE BYE LAWS.

A letter from the Local Government dated 19th April, enclosing draft of the byelaws proposed to be made by the Local Board, was read by the clerk. The letter stated that byelaws framed in accordance with the drafts, and duly adopted by the Local Board might be submitted for confir- mation after the preliminary requirements of section 184 of the Public Health Act, 187, bad &teen adopted. The Local Government Board added that if any objection to the pro- posed byelaws should be made by any person locally in- terested, they woold deem it necessary to consider the ground of the objection.—Mr. Carey proposed, and Dr. O'Keeffe seconded a propositidin that the byelawe, as printed, be approved and adopted subject to the approval of the L0C.41 Government Board, and that after the prescribed notice had been given application ha made to the Local Government Board for confirmation of the byelaws.
IMPROVED V7kTER SOPPLY.-THE ACCIDENT AT _ . STOCKSWELL.

In moving the minutes of the dra-s. and Water Committee, Mr. H. Gaskell said the alterations at Stockswell pumping station were nearly completed, and the engine was working most satisfactorily. At the present time it was pumping 1,400,000 gallons a day, which was double the amount of water pumped before the alterations. Although they had this increased supply of water the water in the well had not lowered at all. (Hear, hear.) The alterations had been made entirely out of the revenue, so that no addition to capital had taken place, and be hoped time would show that they had trebled the supply of water from that place. He was in banes that he should be ab'e te say that the whole wolk had been carried out without an accident occurring, but unfortunately he could not. As they would see by that morning's papers, an accident took place on Sunday, by which a man working for the contractor lost hie life. The whole of the dangerous work had been successfully accom• olished ; this was an accident which might have occurred at any time ; and was in fact not connected with the alter- ations. He was sure that the father and friends of the man would receive the sympathy of the members of the Board, all the more so as ibis was the second son he had lost by accident at the pumping station. He was reminded by Mr. Brown that the selling price of the additional water they would get from the well would amount to £4,500 a year. This was taking the price of water at 5,1, but this did not represent the Board's saving. The saving was in the cost of pumping.—Mr. Wright seconded the motion, which!was carried.—lt was decided to arrange for the annual inspection at the next meeting.

div.head: HEALTH COMMITTEE.
div.p: HEALTH COMMITTEE.

The Medical Officer (Dr. Cooper) reported to this Com- mittee that during April there were 92 births and 44 deaths, being at the rate respectively of 36.8 per 1,000 and 176 per 1,000. There were 12 deaths amongst children under one year, and 4 amonest children between 1 and 5 years. Zynnotic diseases caused three deaths.—Tbe Nuisance In- spector reported that there bad Seen one fatal case of ty- phoid fever and two of diarrhcea. Several cases of measles had been reported; nene so far had proved fatal. A dona- tion of £2 2s having been received from tie Licensed Victualler's Association of St. Helens and Widnes per Mr. W. J. Hargreaves, the Clerk was instructed to thank the Association for the donation.—The receipts from the mar- ket for the month were £4l Os Bd, being an increase, of £5 16e lid as compared with April last vear.—The minutes were adopted on the motion of Dr. O'Keeffe.

A SUNDAY NUISANCE ON THE MARKET GROUND. • Mr. Sadler asked if the Health Committee derived any revenue from netting the Market Ground on &Sunday. Last Sunday morning a photographer managed to make himself a nuisance to all the people coming to and from the churches.—Dr. O'Keeffe replied that the committee did•not let the Market Ground or derive any emolument fromdt last Sunday or any previous Sunday since the market came into the possession of the Board. If a photographer had caused a nuisance he thought it was the duty of the pdlice to interfere rather than tbe Board. He thought the con- servators of the public peace would do their utmost to pre- vent any nuisance occurring on a Sunday either on the Marker Ground or elsewhere —Mr. Sadler said he should like to know if it was not let by the committee on Sundays bow was it let at all. They might gather from the remarks of the doctor that anybody might occupy the ground on a Sunday without paying toll at all —Dr. O'Keeffe said there were no regulations for the Market Ground on Sundays. He thought the matter would be best left in the hands of the police.—Mr. Brown thought the Board was not justified in bringing a nuisance into the tovrt and asking another body to put it &two. The most straightforward manner would be for the committee to say the Market Ground should not be occupied on Sundays.—Dr. O'Keeffe: You might say the same about the Salvation Army. They are considered the biggest nuisance in the place on a Sunday.—Mr. Brown: They do some good and these chaps don't —The Chairman said the best mode would be to move that the matter he considered by the committee. Why not do this instead of grumbling ?—Dr. O'Keeffe : I don't think it is fair of Mr. Brown ti say that we bring these nuisances into the town.—The Chairman was sure it was not the wish of the committee or of any member of the Board to introduce a nuisance.—Mr. Brown moved that t e matter be referred tao the committee, and Dr. O'Keeffe remarked that it should have attention.

div.head: Xettero to the editor.
div.p: Xettero to the editor.
THE JUBILEE CELEBRATION.

Sir,—One so humble in life is almost afraid to speak, but now that one has got great encouragement from so bigh an authority it makes me wiling to vesture. With: regard to this question of celebrating her Majesty's Jubilee, there appears up to now no life in it as far as Warrington is cm- cerned. Everyboy is asking somebody else whether they know anything about it. It is, se to speak, neither der 41 nor al‘ve. I only wish to say now that I read with joy Mr. Alderman Crosfield's remarks at the—Couneil meeting on Tuesday last with reference to the small allowance made to,the children of the'various schools for their treat on that day ; and to express my astonishment that no gentleman bas broken the ice before maw,. By your permission I may have something to say en, this question neat week, but in the meantime the Sunday school managers and teaches who have to stand all the worry and anxiety of that day witl feel a little more hopeful and will look forward to Mr. Alderman Crosfleld to help them out of the slough of de- spond, for 6,1 per head.will not do it.—Yours truly, Warrington, May 13, 1887. 13•D5

div.head: ANOTHER JUBILEE PROPOSAL.
div.p: ANOTHER JUBILEE PROPOSAL.

was very pleased to read "Assistant's" letter respecting the shops half-holiday scheme. Like him, I can- not understand why, if a half-holiday per week is good for thelwholesale. it should not also be good for the retail. I am quite sure the work of the latter on the whole is In every way as harrassine and gives as much weariness of mind and_bodv as the former, yea, and in many cases more so.

If tbe movement were properly taken up, and observed by say a dozen Cl the principal establishments in the town (chiefly grocers and drapers), the rest, I believe, would quickly follow suit. Does it not stand to reason that the assistants of both sexes in our large houses of business would be the better in many ways for this little extra recrea- Cori, giving time both for physical exercise and mental im- provement? Without doubt there are the few who would abuse the new departure by over-indulgences and excesses, and they wiuld soon find bow they worsted themselves. But this surely would not be a reason to debar the respect- able and intellectual portion of asssistants from having this great boon. Trusting some gentleman or lady of high social influence in the town will have the goodness to take the matter up, and lend their names in support- of any favourable pro- posals, I remain, yours faithfully, DESIDERATUM,.

div.head: FREE LIBRARY QUESTION.
div.p: THE FREE LIBRARY QUESTION.

Sir,—There are two or three facts in connection with•this library question that, it seems to me, cannot be kept tocr constantly and clearly intmind. These are, that the library is a public institution, maintained by the people of the tows as a whole by money compulsorily taken from them in the shape of rate ; that the Town Council has complete con- trol over tha Museum and Library Committee (that is to say it can make or unmake the committee as it likes);. and, finally, that thee Town Council is entirely amenable to the popular vote. This may to some seem needless intormation, bill if they consider the singular impressions many people have with regard to the library they will admit that it is information which needs disseminating. Not a few people look upon the institution in Sold-street as a private, or at all events as a semPprly,ate, concern, under the complete and indisputable *mufti?' o!, ,a. small number of gentlemen, lanae of whom are highly respected and of iniMence in the. toWn. The comparatively small advantages at present deilved from the library they appear to think are due in no mill degree to the generosity and remarkable philanthropy Of the gentlemen who have control. That they themselves, and the rest of their fellow ratepayer, are those who defray the annual expenses of the museum and library when they pal their rates, never enters their heads; nor do they lay hottl of the fact that the gentlemen of the Museum and liirary Committee merely take into their hands the amount which is obtained from a penny rate and spend it, without any outsiders who find the money being allowed to pry into details, pretty much according to their own notions—which may be rather antiquated—of the way in which an institu- tion of the kind ought to be conducted. Asa said at the out- set; it is desirable that these facts should be kept in mind whjon considering the library question, and it this is done there can be little doubt that the demand for fair and equal treatment all round wi.l be irresistible. UNSICUS.

div.head: 'EE RECENT TEMPERANCE MEETING.-A HINT.
div.p: 'EE RECENT TEMPERANCE MEETING.-A HINT.

Sir,—l was one of the large number who attended the temperance demonstration held on Monday evening in the Public Hall, at Warrington, and, although I enjoyed it very ltlnCh, I have a little grumble to give expression to. Very few, of those responsible for the arrangements at public meetings held in Warrington seem to realise that it is pom' sible to have too much of a good thing, and that people who leave their homes to go to a meeting expect to be able to arrive back at something like a reasonable hour. The meet- ing on Monday was brought to a conclusion shortly after ten o'clock, but it would have been considerably later had mot the audience showed most palpably that they had had enough. The chairman had called upon the choir for a glee, and there wen several items on the programme, in. eluding two votes of thanks, n,ot reached, but I should think quite half of those resent rose-tetheir feet and made for the door. The chairthan 4id the best thing poes;ble under she circumstances by bringing the affair to a hurried con- elusion. the' doxology tieing substituted for the intended glee. Surely this should serve as a hint. Much of the blame probably lies in the egregious vanity of many speakers--and particularly reverend enes—who, if called upoistat an early stage of a meeting oftert steal the time of others who intend to speak, and occupy' about three times longer than they should. Consequently succeeding speakers have to make their remarks very concise, or otherwise the meeting is protracted beyond all reason. This is a matter I have often noticed in Warrington. The Wesleyan body were Jay considerate in joining with the Federation at the meetitg on Monday night, and two " reverends " from that body were down for speeches, but as the lively speech of Major Waterston and the dull one of Canon Leigh, with one or two glee!, occupied the time of the meeting until about half•past nine, they had not much chance of letting them- salved off in the usual manner of Wesleyan divines. They are ne.i,t to be held guiltless in natters of this kind, for they generally talk for all they are worth, but this time they reade,the best of a bad job. lam sore It would be far more satisfactory to the public generally if at meetings, religions, political, or otherwise, a certain time was allotted to sack speaker, and it was arranged that, say tea o'clock, should be the latest hoer for Closing.—Yours truly, May 12, 1887. Both were taken to the Infirmary. The wounds, though serious, are not believed to be fatal. FSTITION IN BANKRUPTCY AGAINST LORD COLIN. A petition in bankruptcy has been presented against Lord Colin Campbell. the petitioning creditor being the Doke of Marlborough, who claims £971 in respect of his taxed costs in the recent divorce proceedings. The Act of Bankruptcy alleged is non-compliance with the requirements of a bank- ruptcy notice. Mr. Registrar Giffard has appointed the hearing of the petition for the 23rd inst. MOWN. Lewis and Lewis are the solicitors to the proceedings.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER

LONDON, TilllltsDAlr. Mr. Gladstone has added ic new terror tn. public life. At ordinary times, and wi.th statesmen of ordinary character, the occurrence of great speeches are pretty sorely forecasted.. They are made at public meetings after prolonged notice, or am der delivered in the House of Commons where perma- nent arrangements are made for preserving Them for the public. But such is Mr. Gladstone's energy and enthusiasm in tke cause to which he has devoted the remaining dzys of his life, that no one knows what a day may bring forth. He goes out teb, private dinner, and lot his conversation across the. walnuts and the wine takes the fortn of an impsrt- ant speech some three or four columns long. He goes out to luncheon at a private house, and be- hold! the reading public, who ratherthought Wed- nesday was politically an uneventfed day, opened' their Thursday morning's papers to' find a speech' four columns long. The secret of his deliverance se Dr. Parker's on Wednesday was successfully kept'. _

Arrangements had been privately made with-one'of 1 the news agencies, and miscarriage of what might,.l and did, prove an important statement'was provi- ded against. But the bur columns fell like a thunderbolt in sub-editorial rooms. Ttie new de- parture is very well for Mr. Gladstone, who is relieved from the Btrain2 of addressing an im- mense audience. But it is a little hard on the II newspapers. I am told by one of, the very few outoiders pre- seat that, apart from Mr. Gladstone's presence, the 1 meeting waq a most remarkable one. Thbre were present some fifty of the leading Nonconformist divines, every man the centre of a far-reaching circle of political activity. A singularl^ hard- headed collection of men not -very particular in the matter of dress, and gifted with remarkable staying powers at luncheon. Dr. Parker had hospitably prepared a stupendous firtst set forth in a marquee erected for the occasion in tias. back garden. It seemed as if the whole of the afternoon would be required in getting through theimposing list. But the stalwart divines, doing what they had to do with all their hearts, fell to with a will, and to the undisguised amusement of the *afters the dishes were pretty well cleared within an hour. Mr. Gladstone was in ex' cellent health and spirits, and seemed especially to enjoy the 'company in which, he found hiraself. His reception showed that the great Nonconformist body, represented by the pick of its pulpit power; was-heart and soul with him. Hie voice at the commencement was, as is not unusual, a lfttle husky, but, also according to custom, it cleared as he proceeded, ringing out in trumpet tones as he invited the earnest crowd before limn to "labourtd- gether as one man until the memory of centuriesrof iliLtreatment of Ireland had been effaced." _ .

The House of Cteramons has had another tiff; night sitting, an event which a few years ago used to create a thrill of emotion throughout the coun- try. It is now taken as a matter of ordinary Ptr- liamentary procedure. The Coercion Bill is jolting and rumbling its slow. way, being helped over ruts by liberal' use of the cloture. Mr. Smith has be- come quite an adept in this practice,. though in the course of Mondays all-night sitting he met with a severe rebuff from Mr. Courtney, who, exercising ,sthe privilege of Chairman of Committees, vetoed cone of the successive proposals, for the cloture. 'There never was any real prospect of the Committee stage being covered before Whitsuntide. It seems now that we shall be within measurable distance-of the Prorogation before the Bill leaves the House of Commons. The Coercionists are moderately cheer- ful in the certainty that the Lords wilt make short work,of it. The Radicals in the House of Commons have been for some time in preparation for resistance to the vote of £17,000 to deck up Westminster Abbey for the Jubilee service. The proposal is objectionable from several points of view. In the first place it Is absolutely unnecessary, shibe St. Paul's Cathedral might, at the expenditure of a couple of hundred pounds, be made ready for the occasion. EVen more important—for after all seventeen thousand pounds here or there is nothing in the lodger of the, British nation—the selection of Westminster Abbey' for the festival is another of the almost unbroken series of slights, with which the popular wish has been flouted on this happy occasion.. If St. Paid's were chosen it wouldnecessitate the passage of the- Queen through a long line of leading thoroughfares. and the people would get something for their; money in the shape of a spectacle. But her Majesty,. i it is charitable to believe, n ignorance of the popive lay desire, insists upon going to Westminster Abbey.- Hence much popular disappointment and the ex- penditure of .E 17,000. The same spirit is shown in respect of the visit to the Bast Bad next, Satur- day, though here there is not ground for the hope that her Majesty has erred through ignorance. A numerously signed petition was drawn up suggest,- ing on substantial grounds Cvariation in the day of the visit. The petitemers in due course received a letter from Sir Henry Ponsonby, to the effect that the petition had been brought under the notiee• of- the Queen, who had not made any answer; This. ia a pretty severe snub for a loyal' section of ' the people, who are spending much money anddevoting considerable time to preparing a, hearty reception for a rarely-seen sovereign. The discussion on the vote for Westminster Ab- bey, which stands on the agenda of the Rouse of ' Commons for to-night, is likely to be followed in Committee of Supply by another on somewhat dif- ferent lines. Buckingham Palace, long unused as a residence, is, like Westminster Abbey, now in the hands of the workmen, who are preparing it for the receptien of, something like a hundred of the Queen's guests—foreign kings, queens, princes, and royal people's people. The question, not yet openly mooted, is who is to pay for this work?' In conver- sation in the House of Commons it is conveniently taken for kranted that the Queen wilt at least meet the expenses of the entertaining of herprivate guests. Nothing has been said to the contrary; but no one having any experience of the-way' in which these things are managed really believes that the Queen will pay a penny of the expenditure. It will be, somehow, smuggled into the already hugely- swelled votes on account of the Royal Palaces. But I doubt whether it will escape the eagle eye of the economists below the gangway. One economy that is being effected will certainly ' not meet with objection on the part of the masses, whatever the classes may think of it. It is a fact that the extraordinary touting that has marked the progress of the preparations for the Jubilee has taken the direction of broadly hinting to some members of the aristocracy that any offer made by them to place their houses and establishments at the disposal of the Queen's guests will be favourably received. Two well-known houses have already been thus disposed of. Lord and Lady Breadalbane will give up their quaint old house in Cavendish- square to the King of Sweden and his family,whilst Lord Spencer resigns Spencer House to the Crown Prinee and Princess of Germany. These noble lords have not even been asked to do the honours of their own house. They turn out bag and baggage, and in the very height of the season go and find a tem- porary lodging where they may. The Prince of Wales, who, in addition to being a colonel in the Army, is a barrister learned in the law, has been dining with his fellow-benchers in the Middle Temple. These dinners in hall are much affected by rising young barristers, or rather,young barristers who are going to rise. They obtain at a reasonable price an exceedingly good dinner with a quite liberal allowance of wine. On the grand day of a term, such as that on which the Prince of Wales attended, there are always present a certain number of guests selected from the notabilities of the day. Up to a certain point benchers, guests, veteran barristers, and youths just " Celled" share

But after the' dinner there comes a moment of eeparation, painful at least, in the lower part of the halt Then benchers mid guests file out through the upstanding ran-kg of the liar; and disappear within the patois of a private room. What happens tf2ere is a subject that eseites the keen cariosity of the' budding bar- rister. It is nothing' seditious or even, uncommon. Only a prolongation of the proceedingy over decan- ters of the choicest wine with coffee and cigars to follow. Both the Inner and the Middle Temple have rare cellars, and since. the days whet Boswell went on sircuit barristers have always been ap- preciadver of such opportunities as are pro,ided on "grand" days. • Yet another club las been formed for the special accommodation of the late birds who keep up the tradition of old Bohemian club life in London. It is nothing like the Cialton or the. Reform. Its mem- bers are cbieffy drawn from the Beefsteak, the Gar- rick, and the Costiopolltan. Its locale is the Gins- venor Gallery, and itis only night of meeting' is Sunday. This will.seena shocking to some people. But the "Gallery" men plead that if they meet lie,- , fore midnight on Sunday they make up for it by carrying on the Meeting:Well into Monday morning. The club is only a fortniglit old as yet, and has read_y undergone considerittle changes. On Sunday' week, when it °petted, therrwat at °lye end of the' Gallery a collectiontd aniall tables, each Tended with supper delicacies. tast Sundaynight these were removed, leaving the big rooroof the Galiery with its picture crowded -*ails uneneumbered, The Gal- lery has been thronged on these •trttr nights, but I doubt whether after the novelty.'has worn away it will become a permanent institutiOrt. 11i any case it would be frequented only duzinv the compara- tively short London semen.
